Array methods::Array.from and Array.of.summary: Array.from builds a new array from an iterable or array-like value, optionally mapping its elements. Array.of builds a new array from its arguments, treating every argument as an element.
Array methods::Array.from and Array.of.explanation: Use Array.from when the input is iterable or array-like, optionally transforming each item during creation. Use Array.of when the supplied arguments themselves should become the array's elements; unlike Array(), it treats one numeric argument as an element rather than a length.
Array methods::Array.from and Array.of.syntax:
Array.from(items)
Array.from(items, mapFn)
Array.from(items, mapFn, thisArg)
Array.of()
Array.of(element1)
Array.of(element1, element2)
Array.of(element1, element2, /* …, */ elementN)

parameters.name: items
parameters.description: An iterable or array-like object to convert to an array.

parameters.name: mapFn
parameters.description: Optional function applied to each value before insertion into the result.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional this value used when executing mapFn.

parameters.name: element1, …, elementN
parameters.description: Elements used to create the array.

Array methods::Array.from and Array.of.returns: Both methods return a new Array instance.

example.explanation: The first call converts a Set and transforms each value; the second creates a one-element array without Array()'s single-number special case.

useCases.title: Materialize iterable data
useCases.scenario: Turn a Set, Map, string, or other iterable into an ordinary array.

useCases.title: Normalize array-like values
useCases.scenario: Convert indexed objects with length into arrays.

useCases.title: Map while creating
useCases.scenario: Transform values during conversion instead of calling a separate map pass.

useCases.title: Construct predictable arrays
useCases.scenario: Create arrays containing a single number or a variable argument list without Array() length semantics.

interview.question: What inputs does Array.from support?
interview.answer: Array.from accepts an iterable or an array-like object and returns a new Array instance. It can also apply an optional mapFn to each value while constructing the result.
interview.followUp: How would you convert an async iterable? Use Array.fromAsync rather than Array.from.

interview.question: Why use Array.of instead of Array()?
interview.answer: Array.of places every supplied argument into a new array, including when there is exactly one argument. Thus Array.of(7) produces [7], whereas Array(7) interprets 7 as the desired length.
interview.followUp: What does Array.of() with no arguments return? It returns a new empty Array instance.

interview.question: Are Array.from and Array.of restricted to Array itself?
interview.answer: Both methods are generic factory methods. They can be called with another constructor as this, allowing that constructor to create the resulting instance when it accepts a length argument.
interview.followUp: What happens when an Array subclass inherits of()? The inherited method creates instances of that subclass instead of ordinary Array instances.

keyPoints: Array.from converts supported input into a new shallow-copied array.
Array.of uses its arguments as elements, regardless of how many arguments there are or what types they have.
The optional mapFn transforms each input value before that value is placed in the result.
A mapping callback receives the current element; it can also receive the current index.
Iterable collections such as Map and Set can be passed directly to Array.from.
Array.from is generic and can target a constructor that accepts the new array length.
For a generic Array.of call, the target constructor receives the count of supplied elements.
gotchas: Do not substitute Array(7) for Array.of(7): the former creates an array with length 7, while the latter creates [7].
Array.from is not the async-iterable conversion method; use Array.fromAsync for async iterables.
A plain object without iterable behavior or a length/index structure is not a direct Array.from input.

Array methods::Array.prototype.at.summary: Reads an array element by zero-based index, with negative indexes counting backward from the end. Returns undefined when the requested position is outside the array.
Array methods::Array.prototype.at.explanation: Call `at(index)` on an array. The index is converted to an integer; non-negative values count from the beginning, while negative values are added to the array length to count backward. If the resulting position is outside the array, the method returns `undefined` without reading a corresponding property.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: Zero-based array-element index, converted to an integer. Negative values count from the end.

Array methods::Array.prototype.at.returns: The element in the array matching the given index, or undefined when the computed index is outside the array.

example.title: Reading from either end
example.code:
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];

console.log(colors.at(0));  // "red"
console.log(colors.at(-1)); // "blue"
console.log(colors.at(99)); // undefined
example.explanation: Use a non-negative index from the start or a negative index from the end; an index outside the array returns undefined.

useCases.title: Access the last element
useCases.scenario: Read the most recent item without manually subtracting from length.

useCases.title: Use relative indexing
useCases.scenario: Retrieve an element relative to the array's end using a compact index.

useCases.title: Work with array-like values
useCases.scenario: Read from array-like objects that expose length and integer-keyed properties.

interview.question: How does `Array.prototype.at()` handle negative indexes?
interview.answer: `at(index)` returns the element at a zero-based index. Positive indexes count from the beginning, and negative indexes count backward from the last element.
interview.followUp: What does `at(-1)` do on an empty array? It returns `undefined`, because the computed position is outside the array.

interview.question: How does `at()` differ from bracket notation?
interview.answer: For a non-negative integer, `array.at(index)` and `array[index]` read the same element. `at()` additionally provides relative indexing from the end, which bracket notation does not provide with negative numbers.
interview.followUp: How would you read the last element without `at()`? Use `array[array.length - 1]`.

interview.question: What happens when the index is out of range?
interview.answer: The argument is converted to an integer, then the method reads the array length and determines the property to access. It returns `undefined` when the requested index is below `-array.length` or at least `array.length`.
interview.followUp: Can it be used on an array-like object? Yes, because the method is generic and requires only a length and integer-keyed properties.

keyPoints: `at()` reads and returns the element selected by its integer index.
A negative index counts from the array's end: `-1` is the final element, `-2` the preceding one.
Indexing is zero-based, and the argument is converted to an integer before selection.
For a negative index, the effective position is calculated by adding the index to the array length.
For non-negative integer indexes, `at()` is equivalent to bracket access.
The method uses the receiver's `length` to calculate which property should be read.
gotchas: `array[-1]` does not read the last element: bracket notation treats `-1` as a string property name, so use `array.at(-1)` instead.
Out-of-range indexes return `undefined`; the method does not throw merely because the requested position is unavailable.
The method can be borrowed for array-like objects, provided the receiver has a `length` property and integer-keyed properties.

Array methods::Array.prototype.filter.summary: Creates a new shallow array containing the elements of an array whose predicate returns a truthy value. Elements rejected by the predicate are omitted.
Array methods::Array.prototype.filter.explanation: Call filter with a callback for each assigned array element. The callback receives the element, its index, and the source array; elements whose callback result is truthy are copied into a new shallow array, while other elements are omitted. The optional thisArg supplies the callback's this value.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: A function executed for each assigned element. Return a truthy value to keep the element and a falsy value to omit it; it receives the element, index, and source array.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when callbackFn runs.

Array methods::Array.prototype.filter.returns: A new shallow array containing the elements for which callbackFn returns a truthy value; if none pass, an empty array.

example.title: Keep matching objects
example.explanation: Creates a new array containing only products whose inStock property is truthy.

useCases.title: Extract matching records
useCases.scenario: Select records meeting a condition before rendering or processing them.

useCases.title: Exclude rejected items
useCases.scenario: Remove unwanted values such as inactive entries or failed validations.

useCases.title: Filter array-like data
useCases.scenario: Build a subset from an array-like object with length and integer-keyed properties.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.filter return?
interview.answer: filter returns a new shallow array containing values for which the callback returns a truthy result. It does not include values whose callback result is falsy; if none pass, the result is empty.
interview.followUp: Does filter mutate the source array? No: it constructs a separate result array, although object references inside that result remain shallow copies.

interview.question: What arguments can the filter callback receive?
interview.answer: The callback receives the current element, its index, and the array on which filter was called. An optional thisArg determines the callback's this value.
interview.followUp: What happens with an arrow callback and thisArg? The arrow function's lexical this is not replaced by thisArg.

interview.question: How does filter handle sparse arrays and iteration?
interview.answer: filter invokes the callback once for each array index that has an assigned value, in ascending index order. Empty slots in sparse arrays are skipped.
interview.followUp: Are newly appended elements processed? No; the method establishes the range before the first callback invocation.

keyPoints: The method is iterative: it evaluates the supplied callback for each assigned element in the array.
Passing the predicate keeps the corresponding value in a newly created result array.
The callback can declare the current element, its index, and the source array as arguments.
The optional second argument supplies the callback's this value.
The returned array is shallow, so nested objects are not cloned.
A predicate that rejects every element produces an empty array rather than null or undefined.
gotchas: Sparse-array holes are skipped: the callback does not run for empty slots.
filter can operate on array-like objects when they provide a length and integer-keyed properties.

Array methods::Array.prototype.find and.summary: `find()` returns the first array element whose predicate is truthy; `findLast()` returns the last such element. Both return `undefined` when no element matches.
Array methods::Array.prototype.find and.explanation: Both methods call a predicate for array elements until it returns a truthy value. `find()` examines indexes from lowest to highest, while `findLast()` examines them from highest to lowest; each returns the selected element or `undefined` when no predicate call matches.

parameters.name: predicate
parameters.description: Function invoked for each visited index; its truthy result selects the element. It receives the element, index, and searched array.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as `this` while invoking the predicate.

Array methods::Array.prototype.find and.returns: The first matching element for `find()` or the last matching element for `findLast()`; `undefined` if no element matches.

example.title: Find matching values from either end
example.explanation: The two methods use the same predicate but search in opposite directions, so they can select different matching values.

useCases.title: Locate the first match
useCases.scenario: Choose the earliest matching record, such as the first failed validation.

useCases.title: Locate the last match
useCases.scenario: Choose the most recent matching record, such as the latest event meeting a condition.

useCases.title: Reuse the generic array method
useCases.scenario: Search array-like objects that expose length and integer-keyed properties.

interview.question: What does `Array.prototype.find()` return?
interview.answer: `find()` searches in ascending index order and returns the first element whose predicate result is truthy. If every result is falsy, it returns `undefined`.
interview.followUp: How does `findLast()` differ? It searches in descending index order, returning the highest-index matching element or `undefined`.

interview.question: How does `findLast()` choose its result?
interview.answer: `findLast()` starts at the highest index and invokes the predicate while moving toward index zero. It stops immediately after a truthy result and returns that element.
interview.followUp: What if two elements match? The one at the higher index wins because the search begins at the array's end.

interview.question: What arguments can the predicate receive?
interview.answer: The predicate receives the current element, its index, and the array being searched. An optional `thisArg` supplies the `this` value used while invoking the callback.
interview.followUp: Does the method require a genuine Array? No; the method is generic and only requires a length property plus integer-keyed properties.

keyPoints: `find()` tests elements from index 0 upward and stops at the first truthy predicate result.
`findLast()` tests elements from the highest index downward and stops at the first truthy predicate result.
The returned value is the matching element itself, not its index.
A search with no truthy predicate result produces `undefined`.
The predicate defines a match through JavaScript truthiness rather than requiring the literal boolean `true`.
The callback receives the current element, followed by the current index and searched array.
gotchas: Sparse arrays are not skipped: the predicate runs for every index, and an empty slot is observed like `undefined`.
The array method is generic, so it can operate on array-like objects when called with an appropriate `this` value.

Array methods::Array.prototype.flat and.summary: Array.prototype.flat() returns a new array with nested array elements flattened through a chosen depth. Array.prototype.flatMap() maps each element and flattens each mapped result by one level in the same operation.
Array methods::Array.prototype.flat and.explanation: flat() creates a new array by recursively concatenating nested arrays through the requested depth; without an argument, the depth is 1. flatMap() applies a callback to each present source element and flattens each callback result by one level, so returning an array can add multiple output elements while returning a non-array adds one value.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: The maximum nesting depth to flatten; omitted means 1. Infinity removes all reachable array nesting.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: A callable applied to each present source element. It receives the element, its index, and the source array, and may return an array or a single value.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: The value used as this inside callbackFn.

Array methods::Array.prototype.flat and.returns: Both methods return a new array. flat() contains elements flattened through the requested depth; flatMap() contains callback results flattened by one level.

example.title: Flatten arrays and map in one pass
example.explanation: Use flat() when you need to remove nested array layers, and flatMap() when each source element must first produce a value or array whose contents are flattened one level.

useCases.title: Remove nesting
useCases.scenario: Convert nested collections such as arrays of arrays into one-dimensional results.

useCases.title: Expand or filter during mapping
useCases.scenario: Turn each item into zero, one, or multiple output items.

useCases.title: Collect nested properties
useCases.scenario: Extract and combine arrays stored inside records or objects.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.flat() do, and what is its default depth?
interview.answer: flat() returns a new array and defaults to flattening one level. Its optional depth controls recursive flattening, so flat(Infinity) can flatten all nested array levels.
interview.followUp: What happens with a negative depth? It is converted to a nonpositive depth, so nested arrays are not flattened; the result is still a new array.

interview.question: How does flatMap() differ from map().flat()?
interview.answer: flatMap() maps each present element and then flattens the mapped result by exactly one level. It is equivalent in behavior to map(callbackFn, thisArg).flat(1), while combining the operations can be more efficient.
interview.followUp: Can flatMap() flatten two nested levels? No. The flattening step is fixed at one level; a callback can explicitly reshape or flatten its own output if needed.

interview.question: What callback and receiver behavior should you know for flatMap()?
interview.answer: Both methods return new arrays and are generic: they use the receiver's length and integer-keyed properties. flatMap() requires the callback to be callable and passes the element, its index, and the source array to the callback.
interview.followUp: Does flatMap() flatten any iterable returned by the callback? No. Only an Array result is flattened; non-array results are appended directly.

keyPoints: flat() returns a new array and recursively concatenates nested array elements up to the supplied depth.
flatMap() first transforms each source element with a callback, then builds a new result array.
The observable operation performed by flatMap() matches map(...).flat(1), with the two stages combined.
flatMap() processes the source through an iterative callback-based operation rather than recursively mapping nested input.
flatMap() can operate on array-like receivers that provide length and integer-keyed properties.
These methods create new arrays using the receiver's species constructor when that mechanism applies.
gotchas: Sparse source arrays skip callback execution, so flatMap() does not invoke the mapper for holes.
Holes in arrays being flattened are omitted rather than preserved.
Only actual arrays returned by flatMap() are flattened; array-like or other iterable objects remain single values.
A scalar callback result contributes one element, so return [] to emit nothing and return [value] to emit a value conditionally.

Array methods::Array.prototype.includes.summary: Check whether an array contains a value with includes(), or obtain the first matching position with indexOf(). Their main behavioral difference is that includes() finds NaN, while indexOf() does not.
Array methods::Array.prototype.includes.explanation: Use includes(searchElement, fromIndex) when you need to know whether an array contains a value. Use indexOf(searchElement, fromIndex) when you need the first matching zero-based index; it returns -1 when no match exists. The methods differ in equality: includes() uses SameValueZero and finds NaN, while indexOf() uses strict equality and does not. Both accept an optional starting position.
Array methods::Array.prototype.includes.syntax:
array.includes(searchElement)
array.includes(searchElement, fromIndex)
array.indexOf(searchElement)
array.indexOf(searchElement, fromIndex)

parameters.name: searchElement
parameters.description: The value to search for.

parameters.name: fromIndex
parameters.description: Optional zero-based starting index. Negative values count from the end; values below the negative array length use 0, and values at least the array length prevent a search.

Array methods::Array.prototype.includes.returns: includes() returns true if the value is found and false otherwise. indexOf() returns the first matching index, or -1 if no match exists.

example.title: Membership and position
example.code:
const values = ["a", NaN, "b", undefined];

console.log(values.includes(NaN));          // true
console.log(values.includes("b", 2));       // true
console.log(values.indexOf("b"));           // 2
console.log(values.indexOf(NaN));            // -1
console.log(values.indexOf("missing"));     // -1
example.explanation: Use includes() for a boolean membership test and indexOf() when the first matching position is needed.

useCases.scenario: You need a true/false answer for whether a value occurs in an array.

useCases.title: Find a first position
useCases.scenario: You need to branch based on the position of the first occurrence.

useCases.title: Limit the starting position
useCases.scenario: You need to search only a suffix of an array.

interview.question: What is the practical difference between includes() and indexOf()?
interview.answer: includes() returns a boolean indicating whether the value is present. indexOf() returns the first matching zero-based index, or -1 if there is no match.
interview.followUp: Which method can locate NaN? includes() can, because it uses SameValueZero; indexOf() cannot, because it uses strict equality.

interview.question: How does fromIndex affect the search?
interview.answer: Both methods accept an optional fromIndex. A negative value counts backward from the array's end, while searching still proceeds from the computed position toward the end.
interview.followUp: What happens when fromIndex is at least the array length? includes() returns false without searching; indexOf() returns -1.

interview.question: How do the comparison rules differ?
interview.answer: includes() uses SameValueZero: it behaves like strict equality except that NaN equals NaN, while -0 and +0 are equal. indexOf() uses strict equality, so NaN is never found.
interview.followUp: How do sparse arrays differ? includes() visits holes as undefined, whereas indexOf() skips empty slots.

keyPoints: includes() compares values with SameValueZero, so it recognizes NaN and treats negative zero and positive zero as equal.
indexOf() uses the same comparison as === and returns the earliest matching index.
indexOf() communicates absence with -1, making it suitable when the element's position matters.
A negative fromIndex is measured from the array's end before the forward search begins.
Even after a negative starting position is calculated, the search direction remains forward.
gotchas: indexOf() cannot find NaN because its strict-equality comparison treats NaN as unequal to itself.
includes() can match an empty slot when searching for undefined; sparse-array holes are treated as undefined.
indexOf() does not inspect empty slots in sparse arrays, so a hole is not treated as an undefined element.
For includes(), a starting index at or beyond the array length immediately produces false.

Array methods::Array.prototype.join.summary: Array.prototype.join() creates a string by concatenating an array's elements with a chosen separator. It uses a comma by default and returns an empty string for an empty array.
Array methods::Array.prototype.join.explanation: Call join with an optional separator to convert the array's indexed elements to strings and concatenate them in order. Without an argument it uses a comma; null, undefined, and empty slots contribute no text but still preserve their positions.

parameters.name: separator
parameters.description: A string inserted between each pair of adjacent array elements. If omitted or undefined, a comma is used.

Array methods::Array.prototype.join.returns: A string containing all array elements joined with the selected separator; an empty array returns an empty string.

example.title: Joining array values
example.explanation: The first call uses a custom separator; the second shows that null becomes an empty field.

useCases.title: Format a list
useCases.scenario: Convert a list of values into delimiter-separated text for display or logging.

useCases.title: Create delimited data
useCases.scenario: Build a delimited field for simple text output when values are already suitable for string conversion.

useCases.title: Represent nested values
useCases.scenario: Render nested array values as readable text using the default nested comma behavior.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.join return, and what is its default separator?
interview.answer: join returns a string made by converting array elements and concatenating them with a separator. The separator defaults to a comma when omitted, and an empty array produces an empty string.
interview.followUp: What happens for null and undefined elements? They contribute empty strings, so the surrounding separators remain but the value text is absent.

interview.question: How does join behave with sparse arrays?
interview.answer: It visits positions up to the array-like length. Missing positions are treated like undefined, so they generate no element text while still affecting separator placement.
interview.followUp: Can join be used with a non-array object? Yes: the method is generic and needs a length property plus integer-keyed properties.

interview.question: How are nested arrays handled?
interview.answer: join recursively stringifies nested arrays. Because nested calls use their default comma separator, an outer custom separator cannot change separators at deeper levels.
interview.followUp: What does array toString do? It invokes join with no arguments, which makes nested output appear as comma-separated text.

keyPoints: The result is always a newly produced string containing the array's elements in index order.
Calling join() with no argument inserts commas between adjacent elements.
The optional separator is placed between neighboring element positions, not before the first or after the last.
An array with no elements yields an empty string regardless of the separator.
Sparse arrays retain their length-based positions; holes behave like undefined during joining.
Array.prototype.join can operate on array-like objects when they provide length and integer-keyed properties.
gotchas: Null, undefined, and sparse-array slots produce empty text rather than their literal names, so separators can appear next to each other.
Array toString delegates to join without a separator, so replacing an instance's join method also changes that instance's string conversion.
Nested arrays are converted recursively, but a separator supplied to the outer call does not affect nested levels.

Array methods::Array.prototype.map.summary: Array.prototype.map() creates a new array by applying a callback to each assigned element of the source array. The callback's return value becomes the matching element in the result.
Array methods::Array.prototype.map.explanation: Call map() with a callback for each present array element. The callback receives the element, its index, and the original array; each returned value becomes the corresponding item in a new array, while the source array remains separate.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: Function called for each assigned element; it receives element, index, and the source array, and its return value supplies an output element.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when callbackFn runs.

Array methods::Array.prototype.map.returns: A new array whose elements are the callback results.

example.title: Transform each array element
example.explanation: Creates a separate object for each price while preserving the input array.

useCases.title: Format or calculate values
useCases.scenario: Convert raw numeric values into display-ready values.

useCases.title: Transform data shape
useCases.scenario: Project records into smaller objects containing only required fields.

useCases.title: Create annotated records
useCases.scenario: Add indexes or derived fields while retaining one output per input element.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.map() return and how does it affect the original array?
interview.answer: map() invokes the callback for each assigned index and returns a new array containing callback results. It does not mutate the source array itself.
interview.followUp: How does map() treat a sparse array? It skips holes and does not invoke the callback for those indexes; corresponding holes remain in the result.

interview.question: What arguments does the map callback receive?
interview.answer: The callback receives the current element, its index, and the array on which map() was called. Its return value becomes one element of the result.
interview.followUp: What happens when the callback omits return? The corresponding result element is undefined.

interview.question: Is Array.prototype.map() limited to actual arrays?
interview.answer: map() is generic: it needs a this value with a length property and integer-keyed properties. It can therefore be applied to suitable array-like objects, not only Array instances.
interview.followUp: What controls the visited indexes? map() reads length and examines nonnegative integer keys below that length.

keyPoints: The method transforms each visited element and collects the callback results in a fresh array.
Each assigned array index is processed at most once during the map operation.
The callback can use the current value, its numeric index, and the original array.
Every callback result occupies one corresponding position in the output.
The return value is an array rather than the callback's final result.
Existing elements are visited; absent indexed properties are not treated as values.
gotchas: Sparse-array holes are skipped rather than passed to the callback, so the resulting array retains corresponding empty slots.
A callback path with no return value places undefined in the new array.
map() can operate on array-like objects when the this value supplies length and integer-keyed properties.
The iteration uses the length obtained from the source, so later length changes do not extend the traversal.

Array methods::Array.prototype.reduce.summary: Array.prototype.reduce() runs a callback from left to right, carrying each callback result into the next call. It returns the final accumulated value, allowing an array to be folded into one result.
Array methods::Array.prototype.reduce.explanation: reduce() processes present array elements from left to right. The callback receives the accumulated result, the current element, its index, and the array; its returned value becomes the accumulator for the next call, and the final accumulator is returned.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: A function called once for each applicable array element. It receives accumulator, currentValue, currentIndex, and array, and must return the next accumulated value.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: Optional starting accumulator. When supplied, reduction begins with the first array element; otherwise the first present element initializes the accumulator.

Array methods::Array.prototype.reduce.returns: The final accumulated value returned by the last callback invocation, or the sole element when no initialValue is supplied to a one-element array.

example.title: Sum values with an initial accumulator
example.explanation: Adds each order amount to an explicitly initialized running total.

useCases.title: Aggregate values
useCases.scenario: Compute a numeric total, product, or other aggregate from a sequence.

useCases.title: Accumulate structured data
useCases.scenario: Build a derived object such as a frequency table while traversing records.

useCases.title: Fold into one output
useCases.scenario: Combine array elements into a single formatted or transformed result.

interview.question: What arguments does the reducer callback receive?
interview.answer: The callback receives the previous accumulated value, the current element, its index, and the traversed array. Its return value becomes the accumulator for the next callback invocation, and the last accumulator is reduce()'s result.
interview.followUp: What changes when initialValue is omitted? The first present element becomes the accumulator, and processing begins with the next present element.

interview.question: How does initialValue affect the first callback call?
interview.answer: With initialValue, the first callback receives that value as previousValue and the first array value as currentValue. Without it, the first array value is previousValue and the second is currentValue.
interview.followUp: What happens for an empty array without initialValue? reduce() throws a TypeError because no accumulator can be established.

interview.question: Does reduce() mutate the array or observe later changes?
interview.answer: reduce() does not directly mutate its receiver. However, callback code can mutate the array or other referenced objects, and traversal uses the range established when reduction starts.
interview.followUp: Are appended elements processed? No; elements appended after reduction begins are not visited.

keyPoints: The method collapses the processed array elements into one final value.
Reduction proceeds in ascending index order over elements that are present.
Each callback result becomes the accumulator supplied to the next invocation.

Array methods::Array.prototype.slice and.summary: Use `slice()` to copy a range into a new shallow array without mutation. Use `splice()` to remove, replace, or insert elements in the existing array and receive the deleted elements.
Array methods::Array.prototype.slice and.explanation: Use `slice(start, end)` to create a shallow copy of the range from `start` through just before `end`; it leaves the source unchanged. Use `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` to mutate the source by deleting elements and inserting supplied items at the same position; it returns the deleted elements.
Array methods::Array.prototype.slice and.syntax:
slice()
slice(start)
slice(start, end)

splice(start)
splice(start, deleteCount)
splice(start, deleteCount, item1)
splice(start, deleteCount, item1, item2)
splice(start, deleteCount, item1, item2, /* …, */ itemN)

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Zero-based index at which to start extraction, converted to an integer. Negative values count from the end; omitted `start` defaults to 0.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: Zero-based index at which to end extraction, converted to an integer; extraction stops before this index. If omitted, extraction continues to the end.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Zero-based index at which to start changing the array, converted to an integer; negative values count from the end.

parameters.name: deleteCount
parameters.description: Number of elements to remove from `start`.

parameters.name: item1 … itemN
parameters.description: Elements to insert beginning at `start`.

Array methods::Array.prototype.slice and.returns: `slice()` returns a new array containing the extracted elements. `splice()` returns an array containing the deleted elements; it is empty when none are removed.

example.title: Copy versus mutate
example.explanation: `slice()` copies the selected range without changing the original; `splice()` removes and inserts elements in the original array.

useCases.title: Non-mutating extraction
useCases.scenario: Create a subsection or shallow copy while preserving the source array.

useCases.title: In-place deletion
useCases.scenario: Remove one or more elements and inspect what was deleted.

useCases.title: In-place replacement
useCases.scenario: Replace a range with a different number of elements.

useCases.title: In-place insertion
useCases.scenario: Insert elements at the beginning, middle, or end of an array.

keyPoints: `slice()` creates a new shallow-copy array from a selected portion of the source.
The range starts at `start` and stops before `end`, so the end boundary is exclusive.
Calling `slice()` does not change the source array.
`splice()` can delete, replace, and insert elements directly in the source array.
The return value of `splice()` is an array containing the elements it removed.
Negative `start` values count backward from the array's end.
Additional `splice()` arguments are inserted at the change position.
gotchas: `slice()` is non-mutating, but `splice()` changes the original array in place.
Do not use `splice()` when the original array must remain unchanged; use `slice()` or `toSpliced()` instead.
`splice()` always returns an array, including an empty array when nothing was deleted.
Sparse arrays remain sparse in the copied range; missing indexes are not converted into explicit `undefined` values.

Array methods::Array.prototype.some and.summary: some() tests whether at least one array element passes a predicate; every() tests whether all tested elements pass it. Both stop as soon as the result is known.
Array methods::Array.prototype.some and.explanation: Call some() or every() with a predicate. The predicate receives each present element, its index, and the original array; some() stops and returns true at the first truthy result, while every() stops and returns false at the first falsy result. If no decisive result appears, some() returns false and every() returns true.
Array methods::Array.prototype.some and.syntax:
some(callbackFn)
some(callbackFn, thisArg)
every(callbackFn)
every(callbackFn, thisArg)

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: A function executed for each element; it should return a truthy value for a passing element and a falsy value otherwise. It receives element, index, and array.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when callbackFn executes.

Array methods::Array.prototype.some and.returns: some() returns true if callbackFn returns a truthy value for at least one tested element; otherwise false. every() returns false when callbackFn returns a falsy value for a tested element; otherwise true.

example.title: Test array conditions
example.explanation: The first call checks whether at least one score is 100; the second checks whether every score is at least 50.

useCases.title: Check whether all values meet a rule
useCases.scenario: Validate input before processing it.

useCases.title: Check whether any value qualifies
useCases.scenario: Detect a matching condition efficiently.

useCases.title: Reuse predicates beyond arrays
useCases.scenario: Work with array-like objects.

interview.question: How do some() and every() differ?
interview.answer: some() returns true as soon as the predicate returns a truthy value; otherwise it returns false after the applicable elements are checked. every() returns false at the first falsy predicate result; otherwise it returns true.
interview.followUp: What happens for an empty array? some() returns false because no element satisfies the predicate, while every() returns true because no element violates it.

interview.question: What arguments does the predicate receive?
interview.answer: The predicate is called with the current element, its index, and the array being processed. An optional thisArg supplies the callback's this value.
interview.followUp: Are holes in a sparse array tested? No. The callback runs only for indexes that have assigned values.

interview.question: What iteration behavior should you know?
interview.answer: Both methods short-circuit, so they avoid processing later elements once their result is certain. They process the array in ascending index order and use only the initially established range of elements.
interview.followUp: Can they be used with non-array objects? Yes. These methods are generic and require a length property plus integer-keyed properties.

keyPoints: every() verifies that no tested element fails the predicate.
every() short-circuits on its first failure.
The predicate controls whether every() can terminate early.
gotchas: Sparse-array holes are skipped rather than passed to the predicate.
An empty array makes every() return true, so there is no counterexample to find.
The method can operate on array-like objects when the this value has length and integer-keyed properties.

Array methods::Array.prototype.sort and.summary: sort() orders an array in place and returns the same array. toSorted() performs the ordering on a new array, leaving the original unchanged.
Array methods::Array.prototype.sort and.explanation: sort() rearranges an array in place and returns that same array reference. toSorted() applies the ordering without changing the source, returning a new array; pass a comparator for numeric or custom ordering because the default compares string representations by Unicode code points.

parameters.name: compareFn
parameters.description: Optional function that determines element order. If omitted, elements are converted to strings and compared by Unicode code point value.

Array methods::Array.prototype.sort and.returns: sort(): the original array reference, sorted in place. toSorted(): a new array containing the sorted elements.

example.title: Copying versus mutating sort
example.explanation: Use toSorted() when the original array must remain unchanged; use sort() when in-place mutation is intended.

useCases.title: Immutable transformations
useCases.scenario: You need to preserve the source array while producing ordered data.

useCases.title: Numeric sorting
useCases.scenario: You need numeric ordering rather than default string ordering.

useCases.title: Domain-specific ordering
useCases.scenario: You want to sort records using a selected field or custom rule.

interview.question: What is the difference between sort() and toSorted()?
interview.answer: sort() mutates the receiver and returns its reference, whereas toSorted() creates and returns a new sorted array. Therefore, sort() is appropriate when in-place mutation is desired, while toSorted() preserves the original.
interview.followUp: How would you sort numerically without mutating? Call toSorted((a, b) => a - b).

interview.question: How does the comparator affect ordering?
interview.answer: With no comparator, array elements are converted to strings and compared by Unicode code point order. A comparator receives two elements and should return a negative number, a positive number, or zero to express their relative order.
interview.followUp: What happens if the comparator argument is a non-function? The method throws a TypeError.

interview.question: What behavior matters when using toSorted() with array-like or sparse data?
interview.answer: toSorted() is a copying method: it creates a new array and writes the sorted elements into it, leaving the source unchanged. It is generic and relies on a length property plus integer-keyed properties.
interview.followUp: How does it handle sparse arrays? It reads holes as undefined and sorts those values to the end.

keyPoints: sort() mutates the existing array and returns that same array object.
toSorted() is the non-mutating counterpart to sort().
toSorted() returns a distinct array whose elements are ordered ascendingly.
The optional compareFn defines custom ordering, including numeric and property-based sorting.
toSorted() can operate on array-like objects that provide length and integer-indexed properties.
gotchas: Without a comparator, numeric values are ordered as strings, so values such as 10 can appear before 2.
Sparse-array holes are treated like undefined by toSorted(), placed at the end, and do not invoke the comparator.

Async JavaScript::AbortController.summary: AbortController coordinates cancellation for one or more web requests or other supported asynchronous operations. Give an operation the controller’s signal, then call abort() to request cancellation.
Async JavaScript::AbortController.explanation: AbortController owns an AbortSignal that asynchronous operations can observe. Pass the signal to a supported operation such as fetch, and call abort() through the controller to request cancellation; fetch rejects with AbortError, and response-body consumption can also be interrupted.

example.title: Cancel a fetch request
example.explanation: Pass the controller's signal to fetch, then call abort() to cancel the request. The rejected promise is handled as an AbortError.

useCases.title: Cancel a fetch request
useCases.scenario: A user navigates away or presses Cancel while a network request is pending.

useCases.title: Share one cancellation signal
useCases.scenario: Several supported operations should stop together when a lifecycle ends.

useCases.title: Cancel stream processing
useCases.scenario: A consumer must stop processing a response stream.

interview.question: How does AbortController cancel asynchronous work?
interview.answer: Create an AbortController, pass its signal to the asynchronous operation, and call abort() on the controller when cancellation is needed. The signal is the communication channel between the controller and the operation.
interview.followUp: How can one controller affect several operations? Pass the same signal to each operation; aborting the controller communicates cancellation to all operations that support that signal.

interview.question: What does AbortController.signal provide?
interview.answer: The signal property returns an AbortSignal. For fetch, supplying that signal makes the request cancelable, and abort() can also stop response-body consumption and streams.
interview.followUp: What should code do after cancellation? Catch the operation's cancellation error, such as fetch's AbortError, rather than treating it as an unrelated failure.

interview.question: What happens when abort() is called?
interview.answer: Calling abort() aborts an asynchronous operation before it completes. With fetch, the associated promise rejects with an AbortError exception.
interview.followUp: Can cancellation occur after fetch resolves? Yes; aborting before the response body is read can cause body-reading operations to reject with AbortError.

keyPoints: A controller can coordinate cancellation for one or more web requests.
Operations receive the signal as the cancellation communication channel.
Instantiate the controller with the AbortController constructor.
Read signal to obtain the AbortSignal passed to cancelable work.
Call abort() to request cancellation before asynchronous work finishes.
The documented cancellation scope includes fetch requests, response-body consumption, and streams.

Async JavaScript::Iterables and generato.summary: JavaScript iteration protocols let objects expose lazy synchronous or asynchronous sequences. Generators produce values with yield, while async generators and for await...of support promise-based iteration.
Async JavaScript::Iterables and generato.explanation: An iterable supplies an iterator through Symbol.iterator, while an async iterable supplies one through Symbol.asyncIterator. Generator functions pause at yield and resume when next is requested; async generators combine this lazy behavior with await, and for await...of consumes either async iterables or synchronous iterables.

example.title: Lazy asynchronous transformation
example.explanation: The async generator consumes values lazily and yields each value doubled.

useCases.title: Lazy sequence generation
useCases.scenario: Process large or unbounded sequences without storing every value.

useCases.title: Asynchronous data pipelines
useCases.scenario: Transform values from a stream or other asynchronous source as they arrive.

useCases.title: Custom iterable APIs
useCases.scenario: Make custom domain objects compatible with for...of, spread, destructuring, or yield*.

useCases.title: Unified iteration
useCases.scenario: Consume synchronous and asynchronous sources through a consistent loop form.

interview.question: What distinguishes an iterable from an iterator?
interview.answer: An iterable implements Symbol.iterator and returns an iterator. An iterator exposes next(), whose result describes the next value and whether iteration is complete. for...of obtains the iterator and repeatedly requests values until done is true.
interview.followUp: How does asynchronous iteration differ? An async iterable implements Symbol.asyncIterator, and iterator method results are wrapped in promises; for await...of awaits those results.

interview.question: How does yield make generators lazy?
interview.answer: A generator function returns a Generator object when called rather than executing immediately. Each next() resumes it until yield or completion, so yielded values are produced on demand.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for infinite sequences? Because only requested values are computed, allowing a consumer to stop without materializing the entire sequence.

interview.question: How do async generators and for await...of work together?
interview.answer: An async generator is declared with async function*. It can use both await and yield, returns an AsyncGenerator, and its next() calls resolve to iterator result objects; for await...of can consume it.
interview.followUp: Can for await...of consume a synchronous iterable? Yes; it supports both async iterables and sync iterables, unlike for...of, which supports only sync iterables.

keyPoints: An object becomes synchronously iterable by providing Symbol.iterator, whose method returns the iterator used to traverse it.
for...of, spread syntax, destructuring, and yield* request iterable input, so custom objects can participate by implementing the protocol.
Generators support lazy pipelines: each requested value is calculated only when the consumer advances iteration.
Async iterables expose Symbol.asyncIterator, a zero-argument method that returns an async iterator.
Async iterator operations produce promises, allowing iteration to coordinate asynchronous work.
gotchas: A sync-only consumer such as for...of or spread cannot consume an object that implements only the async iterable protocol; use for await...of instead.
Async iterables are consumed by for await...of or by yield* inside an async generator, not by an ordinary synchronous generator.
Calling a generator creates the iterator without running its body; work starts only when iteration requests a value.

Async JavaScript::Promise combinators.summary: Promise combinators coordinate concurrent asynchronous operations. Choose all() for universal success, allSettled() to inspect every outcome, any() for the first success, or race() for the first settlement.
Async JavaScript::Promise combinators.explanation: Promise combinators take an iterable of values or promises and return one promise whose settlement rule depends on the method: require every operation, observe every outcome, finish at the first settlement, or finish at the first fulfillment. The input operations begin concurrently; the combinator does not cancel the remaining work when its returned promise settles.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: An iterable containing promises, thenables, or ordinary values accepted by the selected combinator.

Async JavaScript::Promise combinators.returns: A Promise whose fulfillment or rejection behavior depends on the selected combinator.

example.title: Inspect every outcome
example.explanation: Runs independent requests concurrently and reports each outcome without stopping when one request fails.

useCases.title: Require an aggregate success with all()
useCases.scenario: Several dependent requests must all succeed before rendering a page.

useCases.title: Audit every result with allSettled()
useCases.scenario: Independent jobs should all finish so successes and failures can be logged or summarized.

useCases.title: Use any() for fallback providers
useCases.scenario: Multiple equivalent providers are queried and the first successful response is sufficient.

useCases.title: Use race() for first settlement
useCases.scenario: A request competes with a timeout promise, or the earliest completion determines the next step.

interview.question: How do Promise.all() and Promise.allSettled() differ?
interview.answer: Promise.all() fulfills only after every input fulfills and rejects as soon as any input rejects. Promise.allSettled() instead fulfills after every input has settled and reports each outcome.
interview.followUp: When should allSettled() replace all()? Use it when operations are independent or every individual result must be inspected; use all() when the aggregate requires universal success.

interview.question: Compare Promise.any() with Promise.race().
interview.answer: Promise.any() fulfills when the first input fulfills and rejects only when all inputs reject. Promise.race() settles when the first input settles, so its first result may be either fulfillment or rejection.
interview.followUp: What happens if every input to any() rejects? The returned promise rejects, whereas race() can reject from the first rejection without waiting for the rest.

interview.question: Do promise combinators execute tasks sequentially?
interview.answer: All four methods start their input promises concurrently rather than making each await the previous one. The returned promise applies the method's completion rule to those already-started operations.
interview.followUp: Does settling the aggregate cancel unfinished work? No; the documentation states that concurrent operations continue even when an aggregate result is already available.

keyPoints: The four standard combinators are all(), allSettled(), any(), and race().
all() requires universal fulfillment and fails at the first rejection.
allSettled() waits for every input to finish, whether it fulfills or rejects.
any() selects the first successful input, but has no success result if every input fails.
race() adopts the first settlement, including either a fulfillment or a rejection.
Passing already-created promises lets the operations proceed concurrently while the combinator observes them.
gotchas: A rejection from Promise.all() does not stop the other operations; it only makes their outcomes unavailable through the returned promise.

Async JavaScript::Promises and async.summary: Promises model the eventual success or failure of asynchronous work. Compose them with then, catch, finally, and async/await; cancellation requires stopping the underlying operation, commonly with AbortController.
Async JavaScript::Promises and async.explanation: Promises represent eventual success or failure. An async function always produces a promise; await unwraps a settled promise or throws its rejection inside the function. Use then, catch, or finally to compose follow-up work, and use AbortController when the underlying operation supports cancellation.
Async JavaScript::Promises and async.returns: An async function returns a Promise.

example.title: Await a request and cancel its underlying operation
example.explanation: The async function returns a promise, and await pauses that function until the fetch promise settles. Promise handlers run asynchronously after the current event-loop turn; AbortController cancels the underlying fetch rather than the promise itself.

useCases.title: Sequential asynchronous workflows
useCases.scenario: Fetch data and transform it in sequence while keeping error handling centralized.

useCases.title: Concurrent work
useCases.scenario: Run independent promise operations together and process their combined results.

useCases.title: Cancellation of underlying work
useCases.scenario: Stop a fetch or similar supported operation when a view closes or a request becomes obsolete.

useCases.title: Reliable asynchronous cleanup
useCases.scenario: Attach cleanup that runs whether an operation fulfills or rejects.

interview.question: What is a Promise?
interview.answer: A Promise represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value. It can be fulfilled or rejected, and handlers attached with then, catch, or finally react after settlement.
interview.followUp: What happens if a then handler throws? The promise returned by then becomes rejected with that thrown error, allowing later catch handlers to process it.

interview.question: How do async and await relate to promises?
interview.answer: An async function returns a promise. Await suspends execution of that function until the awaited promise settles; a fulfillment supplies the value, while a rejection is thrown at the await expression.
interview.followUp: Can await block the JavaScript thread? No: it suspends only the async function, allowing the current event-loop work to finish and other work to proceed.

interview.question: How is cancellation handled with promises?
interview.answer: Promises do not define cancellation. To stop work, cancel the underlying operation when its API supports it, commonly by passing an AbortSignal created by AbortController.
interview.followUp: What if the underlying operation cannot be cancelled? The promise remains observable and may settle later, so ignore its result safely and avoid treating promise-handler removal as cancellation.

keyPoints: A promise is a handle for a future result: it eventually becomes fulfilled or rejected.
Chain then for success transformations, catch for rejection handling, and finally for cleanup that should run after settlement.
Within an async function, await pauses that function and resumes with a value or throws the rejection.
An async function starts synchronously until its first await, then later continuation proceeds asynchronously.
Handlers attached to a promise execute in registration order after the relevant settlement.
Use AbortSignal to stop supported underlying work when a pending result is no longer needed.
gotchas: Calling a promise method cannot cancel the operation; cancel the underlying API with a mechanism such as AbortController.
A then callback is not run immediately, even when its promise is already settled.
An async function containing await completes asynchronously, so callers must handle its returned promise.

ES2026 additions::Array.fromAsync.summary: Array.fromAsync() collects an async iterable, iterable, or array-like value into a new array and returns a promise for it. It preserves iteration order while optionally transforming each element.
ES2026 additions::Array.fromAsync.explanation: Array.fromAsync() consumes an async iterable, ordinary iterable, or array-like value and produces a promise for a new array. It processes elements in order; for non-async iterables, elements and mapper results are awaited before they are stored.
ES2026 additions::Array.fromAsync.syntax:
Array.fromAsync(items)
Array.fromAsync(items, mapFn)
Array.fromAsync(items, mapFn, thisArg)

parameters.name: items
parameters.type: async iterable, iterable, or array-like object
parameters.description: An async iterable, iterable, or array-like object to convert to an array.

parameters.name: mapFn
parameters.description: Optional function invoked for each element; its result is used after awaiting.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when invoking mapFn.

ES2026 additions::Array.fromAsync.returns: A Promise whose fulfillment value is a new Array instance.

example.title: Collect and transform an async iterable
example.explanation: Consumes an async generator, awaits each non-async-iterator value, applies the mapper, and resolves to an array in iteration order.

useCases.title: Materialize asynchronous data
useCases.scenario: An API exposes results through an async generator or ReadableStream-like async source.

useCases.title: Transform while collecting
useCases.scenario: Each source item needs asynchronous normalization or conversion before collection.

useCases.title: Collect ordinary or array-like inputs
useCases.scenario: A Set, Map, or array-like object contains values that may be promises.

interview.question: What does Array.fromAsync() return and what inputs can it consume?
interview.answer: It returns a Promise that fulfills with a new Array instance. The source may be an async iterable, iterable, or array-like object, and values are collected in input order.
interview.followUp: How does it choose the source protocol? It uses async iteration when available; otherwise it falls back to ordinary iteration and finally supports array-like objects.

interview.question: How are values and mapFn results awaited?
interview.answer: For a non-async iterable, each element is awaited before insertion. If a mapper exists, its result is also awaited, so asynchronous transformation functions can be used directly.
interview.followUp: What happens when the source is an async iterable? Each yielded value is passed through as-is, so a promise contained in that value is not additionally awaited.

interview.question: What are mapFn and thisArg used for?
interview.answer: The method accepts an optional mapper and optional thisArg. The mapper runs for every element, and its returned value becomes the corresponding array element after awaiting.
interview.followUp: Why can Array.fromAsync() be preferable to Promise.all()? It supports async iteration and sequentially consumes the source in iteration order rather than requiring all values to be available as an ordinary collection first.

keyPoints: It creates a new shallow array from an async iterable, ordinary iterable, or array-like source.
Async sources are consumed using behavior similar to for await...of.
The result is a promise that fulfills with the newly created array.
The mapper's result is awaited before becoming the output element.
Typical async sources include ReadableStream objects and async generators.
gotchas: Promises contained inside the yielded value of an async iterator are not automatically awaited; the promise itself can appear in the resulting array.
Elements from an ordinary iterable are awaited, unlike promise values nested in the yielded value of an async iterator.

ES2026 additions::Error.isError.summary: Error.isError(value) reliably checks whether a value carries the built-in Error brand. Unlike instanceof Error, it works across realms and also recognizes DOMException instances.
ES2026 additions::Error.isError.explanation: Call Error.isError(value) to perform a branded check for an Error value. Unlike instanceof Error, it recognizes Error objects from another realm and rejects objects that merely inherit from Error.prototype; it also returns true for DOMException instances.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to be checked.

ES2026 additions::Error.isError.returns: true if value is an Error; otherwise, false.

example.title: Recognize and normalize a caught value
example.explanation: The caught value is recognized as error-like, including a DOMException, and non-error values could be normalized to an Error.

useCases.title: Cross-realm error detection
useCases.scenario: A library receives values from iframes, workers, or other execution contexts.

useCases.title: Normalize caught values
useCases.scenario: A catch block must handle arbitrary thrown values consistently.

useCases.title: Reject forged error-like objects
useCases.scenario: Code must distinguish genuine errors from objects that only mimic Error through their prototype.

interview.question: What does Error.isError return and what kind of check does it perform?
interview.answer: Error.isError(value) returns a boolean indicating whether value is a built-in Error instance. It performs a branded check rather than relying on the object's prototype chain.
interview.followUp: Why can it recognize cross-realm errors? The check is based on the Error brand, while instanceof compares constructor identity and can fail across realms.

interview.question: Why is Error.isError preferable to instanceof Error?
interview.answer: It is safer than instanceof Error for cross-realm values. It rejects objects that only inherit from Error.prototype and accepts Error objects created under a different realm.
interview.followUp: What is a practical cross-realm source? An Error received from an iframe or another window can have a different Error constructor identity.

interview.question: How does Error.isError treat DOMException?
interview.answer: Error.isError(new DOMException()) returns true. DOMException is treated as an Error for branded-checking purposes even though its constructor is not a normal subclass of Error.
interview.followUp: Would instanceof Error necessarily agree? No; DOMException's prototype relationship does not make it a conventional Error subclass.

keyPoints: Use the static method to obtain a boolean classification of a candidate value.
The implementation-level concept is an internal brand established by Error construction.
Errors from iframes or other execution contexts remain recognizable.
Prototype manipulation alone cannot forge a valid Error value.
DOMException is included in the method's recognized error set.
It supports catch-block handling where thrown values may need consistent error normalization.
gotchas: DOMException is accepted even though it is not specified as a conventional subclass of Error.
Adding Error.prototype to an object's prototype chain does not make that object pass the check.
Do not use instanceof Error when values may originate in another realm.

ES2026 additions::Iterator.concat.summary: Iterator.concat() lazily combines multiple iterable objects into one iterator. It yields each input's values in order without materializing an intermediate array.
ES2026 additions::Iterator.concat.explanation: Iterator.concat() accepts iterable objects and returns an iterator that reads their values sequentially. Consumption is lazy, so values are produced as the result is advanced rather than copied into an intermediate array; each supplied iterable must support the iterable protocol.

parameters.name: it1, it2, …, itN
parameters.description: An object implementing the iterable protocol; pass one or more such objects.

ES2026 additions::Iterator.concat.returns: A new Iterator object that yields the values from each input iterable in sequence.

example.title: Concatenate iterables lazily
example.code:
const numbers = Iterator.concat([1, 2], new Set([3, 4]));
console.log([...numbers]); // [1, 2, 3, 4]
example.explanation: The resulting iterator consumes each iterable in order and produces one combined sequence.

useCases.title: Sequential stream processing
useCases.scenario: Process several collections as one stream while preserving their order.

useCases.title: Memory-conscious composition
useCases.scenario: Combine iterable sources without allocating a merged array first.

useCases.title: On-demand consumption
useCases.scenario: Chain finite data with an iterator source and consume only the required prefix.

interview.question: What does Iterator.concat() return?
interview.answer: It is a static method that returns an Iterator yielding values from its iterable arguments in sequence. Unlike Array.concat(), it does not create a combined array, so consumption remains lazy.
interview.followUp: What happens with an infinite first iterable? Later inputs are never reached, although the combined iterator can continue producing values from the infinite input.

interview.question: What arguments can Iterator.concat() accept?
interview.answer: Each argument must be iterable, meaning it must provide the iterable protocol. An iterator that lacks iterability cannot be supplied directly and should first be adapted with Iterator.from().
interview.followUp: Why is accepting only iterables significant? The method takes ownership of the iterators and can close open iterators when it exits.

interview.question: Can the input iterables have different types?
interview.answer: It can combine iterables of different types because it consumes their iterable protocols rather than requiring a common collection type. The output is still one iterator whose values follow input order.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a large or unbounded number of iterables? Use Iterator.prototype.flatMap() instead of passing them all as arguments.

keyPoints: The static method creates one iterator from multiple iterable inputs.
Values are emitted from the first iterable, then the second, continuing in argument order.
The signature accepts any number of iterable arguments, including a single iterable.
Input values are consumed on demand rather than eagerly copied.
Arrays, sets, and other iterable kinds may be combined.
Built-in iterators are iterable and can therefore be passed directly.
gotchas: An iterator must also implement the iterable protocol; wrap a non-iterable iterator with Iterator.from() before passing it.
If an infinite iterable appears before other inputs, later iterables are unreachable.
Every argument must provide [Symbol.iterator](); ordinary non-iterable values cause a TypeError.

Its source property contains the original JSON text for that value, so the reviver can reconstruct precise numbers or inspect their spelling before returning a replacement.

parameters.description: The string to parse as JSON.

parameters.name: reviver

ES2026 additions::JSON.parse source text.returns: The Object, Array, string, number, boolean, or null value corresponding to the given JSON text, after any reviver transformation.

example.explanation: The reviver reads the exact numeric token from context.source and converts it to BigInt before the parsed result is returned.

useCases.title: Exact integer handling
useCases.scenario: Convert oversized JSON integers to BigInt using the original digit sequence.

useCases.title: Token-level validation
useCases.scenario: Validate numeric spelling or distinguish equivalent primitive representations during parsing.

useCases.title: Custom primitive conversion
useCases.scenario: Retain application-specific representations when standard JavaScript parsing would lose precision.

interview.question: What does the third reviver argument provide?
interview.answer: The reviver is called with a key, the parsed value, and, for primitive values, a context object. The context.source property contains the original JSON text for that primitive, allowing a replacement such as BigInt(context.source).
interview.followUp: How can a reviver preserve an integer that exceeds safe Number precision? Return BigInt(context.source) when processing that value, rather than converting the already-rounded Number.

interview.question: Why use context.source instead of the reviver value?
interview.answer: context.source is the original JSON substring representing the primitive value. It lets code inspect or reinterpret the token instead of relying only on the parsed JavaScript value.
interview.followUp: Why is the source token useful for numbers? A JSON number may lose precision when first represented as a JavaScript Number, while its original digits remain available in context.source.

interview.question: When does the reviver affect the parsed result?
interview.answer: JSON.parse(text, reviver) parses the JSON text and then applies the reviver transformation before returning the result. The reviver's return value is used in place of the corresponding parsed value.
interview.followUp: What happens if parsing fails? JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError for text that does not conform to the JSON grammar, so no transformed result is returned.

keyPoints: Read context.source inside a reviver when the exact JSON spelling of a primitive matters.
The third reviver argument is context, and its source property identifies the primitive's original token.
Without a reviver, JSON.parse returns the JavaScript value represented by the input JSON.
gotchas: The context argument is provided for primitive values, not for objects or arrays.
The reviver's returned value replaces the parsed value; it is not merely an observer.
Malformed JSON prevents the reviver from being used because parsing fails first.

ES2026 additions::Map and WeakMap upsert.explanation: These methods combine lookup and conditional insertion. getOrInsert returns the existing value or stores and returns the supplied default; getOrInsertComputed does the same but calls a callback with the key only when no entry exists, making it suitable for expensive defaults.

parameters.description: A function called with key when key is absent; its result is inserted and returned.

example.explanation: The first call inserts a supplied default, while the second computes its default only when the key is absent.

useCases.title: Defer default construction
useCases.scenario: Creating a value is expensive or has side effects.

useCases.title: Compute key-specific entries
useCases.scenario: A derived value depends on the requested key.

interview.question: What does Map.prototype.getOrInsert do?
interview.answer: getOrInsert checks for the key and returns the stored value when present. Otherwise it inserts the supplied default and returns that value.
interview.followUp: Why can getOrInsert still perform unnecessary work? Its default argument is evaluated before the method runs, so use getOrInsertComputed for deferred creation.

interview.question: When should getOrInsertComputed be preferred?
interview.answer: getOrInsertComputed checks the key first. Only when the key is absent does it call the callback with the key, insert the callback result, and return it.
interview.followUp: What happens if the callback returns undefined? That undefined value is still inserted and returned; absence must be distinguished with Map's key lookup semantics.

interview.question: How are object keys matched?
interview.answer: Map object keys are compared by reference rather than by their contents. Therefore, only the same object reference retrieves an earlier entry.
interview.followUp: How does this differ for primitive keys? Primitive keys are compared according to Map's key equality rules, while object identity remains reference-based.

keyPoints: getOrInsertComputed returns the existing value for a key when an entry is already present.
getOrInsert inserts the supplied default only for a missing key, then returns that inserted value.
The computed form expects a callback whose result becomes the value for a missing key.
The callback receives the lookup key as its sole argument.
A missing key causes the callback result to be both stored and returned.
gotchas: Map keys use identity for objects: two separately created objects with the same contents are different keys.
The computed callback receives the original key, so its result can depend on that key.
Use the computed variant when creating the default has a meaningful cost; the ordinary variant evaluates its argument before the call.

ES2026 additions::Promise.try.summary: Promise.try() turns a synchronous callback invocation into a promise. Values fulfill it, thrown errors reject it, and returned promises are adopted, giving mixed synchronous/asynchronous code one rejection-aware flow.
ES2026 additions::Promise.try.explanation: Promise.try() invokes a callback immediately with the supplied arguments. A normal return is resolved, a synchronous throw becomes a rejection, and a returned promise is adopted, so callers can use one promise-based success and failure flow.

Promise.try(func)
Promise.try(func, arg1)
Promise.try(func, arg1, arg2)
Promise.try(func, arg1, arg2, /* …, */ argN)

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: A function invoked synchronously with the remaining arguments; it may return a value, throw, or return a promise.

parameters.name: arg1, arg2, …, argN
parameters.description: Values forwarded to func in order.

ES2026 additions::Promise.try.returns: A Promise that is fulfilled for a synchronous value, rejected for a synchronous throw, or settled according to a returned promise.

example.title: Normalize a synchronous callback
example.explanation: The synchronous parser result becomes a promise, while either a thrown error or an asynchronous return can be handled by the same catch path.

useCases.scenario: Wrapping a parser or validator that may throw synchronously while exposing a promise API.

useCases.title: Mixed synchronous and asynchronous results
useCases.scenario: Calling a function that sometimes returns a plain value and sometimes returns a promise.

useCases.title: Uniform error handling
useCases.scenario: Forwarding callback arguments while handling all failures through one catch path.

interview.question: What happens when the callback returns a value, throws, or returns a promise?
interview.answer: It synchronously calls the callback and creates a promise capability. A synchronous return resolves that promise, while an abrupt completion rejects it; a returned promise is resolved using promise-resolution behavior.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from Promise.resolve(callback())? Promise.resolve(callback()) cannot convert a synchronous throw from evaluating callback() into a rejection, whereas Promise.try() captures that throw.

interview.question: When is the callback executed?
interview.answer: The callback receives arg1 through argN and is called synchronously with those arguments. The result is then resolved into the returned promise.
interview.followUp: Why might synchronous invocation matter? Side effects and exceptions occur before Promise.try() returns, even though consumers observe the promise through normal handlers.

interview.question: Can Promise.try() be used with Promise subclasses?
interview.answer: Promise.try() is generic and supports subclassing. Its this value must be a constructor whose constructor follows the Promise constructor convention, accepting an executor.
interview.followUp: What must a custom subclass constructor support? It must accept the executor and allow that executor to receive resolve and reject functions.

keyPoints: The callback may return a value, throw synchronously, or return a promise.
Arguments passed after the callback are forwarded to it during immediate invocation.
A direct synchronous result produces an already-fulfilled promise.
A synchronous exception is represented as a rejected promise instead of escaping as an ordinary throw.
When the callback returns a promise, the resulting state follows that promise.
It provides a compact expression-oriented alternative to manually placing a synchronous call inside try/catch and resolving or rejecting its outcome.
The method can operate on Promise subclasses when their construction contract is compatible.
gotchas: Do not use Promise.try() to defer callback execution: unlike then(), it calls the callback synchronously.
A native promise returned by the callback can be passed through unchanged rather than wrapped in another native promise.
Calling Promise.try with an invalid receiver can fail; subclasses must provide Promise-compatible construction behavior.
