useCases.title: Null-prototype dictionaries
useCases.scenario: Create dictionary-like objects that do not inherit names or methods from Object.prototype.

useCases.title: Controlled property descriptors
useCases.scenario: Define property attributes such as writability and enumerability while constructing an object.

interview.question: What does Object.create do?
interview.answer: Object.create(proto) returns a new object whose prototype is proto. Passing null creates an object with no prototype.
interview.followUp: How can you verify the result? Use Object.getPrototypeOf(result) and compare it with proto, including null.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the second argument?
interview.answer: The optional propertiesObject argument defines own properties on the new object. Its enumerable own keys provide property descriptors corresponding to Object.defineProperties().
interview.followUp: Why can this matter? Descriptor flags such as writable, enumerable, and configurable determine how each created property behaves.

interview.question: What arguments are valid, and what does the method return?
interview.answer: The first argument may be an object or null. Any other value causes a TypeError, and the returned object has the specified prototype and properties.
interview.followUp: What happens when the prototype is an object? Property lookup can reach that prototype after checking the new object's own properties.

keyPoints: The method creates a fresh object and sets its internal prototype to the supplied object.
The proto parameter determines which object receives inherited property lookups.
The return value combines the chosen prototype with any properties defined through the optional descriptor object.
The optional propertiesObject follows Object.defineProperties-style descriptor semantics.
Passing null deliberately produces a null-prototype object, useful when inherited Object.prototype members are unwanted.
gotchas: The second argument is interpreted as property descriptors, not ordinary property values; omitted descriptor flags therefore use descriptor defaults.
The prototype argument must be an object or null; primitives cause a TypeError.

Object & JSON::Object.defineProperty and.summary: Object.defineProperty() creates or modifies one own property with a descriptor and returns the target object. Descriptors control stored values or accessors plus writability, enumerability, and configurability.
Object & JSON::Object.defineProperty and.explanation: Object.defineProperty() creates or changes one own property using a descriptor. A descriptor chooses either a data form—value plus writable—or an accessor form—get and set—and can also control enumerability and configurability; omitted attributes receive their documented defaults.

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: The object on which to define or modify the property.

parameters.name: prop
parameters.description: The property name, represented by a string or Symbol.

parameters.name: descriptor
parameters.description: An object describing the property, using a data or accessor descriptor.

Object & JSON::Object.defineProperty and.returns: The object on which the property was defined or modified.

example.title: Data and accessor descriptors
example.explanation: The first definition creates a data property with an immutable value that is enumerable but cannot be reconfigured. The second creates an accessor property: its getter computes a value and its setter controls assignment. A descriptor must use either data fields or accessor fields, not both.

useCases.title: Computed and controlled access
useCases.scenario: Expose a computed or validated property without storing a directly readable field.

useCases.title: Hidden metadata
useCases.scenario: Create an internal metadata property that should not appear in ordinary enumeration.

useCases.title: Immutable configuration
useCases.scenario: Lock selected object state against reassignment or reconfiguration.

interview.question: What does Object.defineProperty() do?
interview.answer: Object.defineProperty(target, propertyKey, descriptor) defines a new own property or modifies an existing one, then returns the target object. The descriptor controls the property’s value or accessors and its attributes.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from Reflect.defineProperty()? Reflect.defineProperty() returns a Boolean status, whereas Object.defineProperty() throws a TypeError when definition fails.

interview.question: How do data and accessor descriptors differ?
interview.answer: A data descriptor uses value and optionally writable. An accessor descriptor uses get and/or set; the two descriptor forms cannot be mixed.
interview.followUp: What happens if an accessor has no setter? Assignment cannot store a value through that property, so writes do not invoke a setter because none exists.

interview.question: What do writable, enumerable, and configurable control?
interview.answer: writable controls whether assignment can change a data value, enumerable controls whether the property appears in enumerable-property operations, and configurable controls whether the property can be changed or removed. For properties created by this method, all three default to false.
interview.followUp: Why can a property become difficult to change after creation? A non-configurable property cannot generally have its descriptor freely altered or be deleted, so its initial configuration matters.

keyPoints: It operates on one named property and returns the same target object, enabling chaining or immediate reuse.
Data descriptors represent stored values; writable determines whether assignment may replace that value.
Accessor descriptors expose behavior through get and set functions instead of storing a directly assigned value.
The writable flag applies to data descriptors and governs assignment-based changes.
A data descriptor’s value may be any JavaScript value, including objects and functions.
An accessor setter receives the value supplied by an assignment as its sole argument.
gotchas: New properties default to non-writable, non-enumerable, and non-configurable, unlike ordinary object-literal properties.
Do not combine data fields such as value or writable with accessor fields such as get or set.
The descriptor argument must describe the property; passing a non-object descriptor causes an error.

Object & JSON::Object.freeze and Object..summary: Object.seal fixes an object's shape while leaving writable existing values changeable. Object.freeze also fixes the shape but makes existing properties non-writable and non-configurable.
Object & JSON::Object.freeze and Object..explanation: Both methods operate on the object itself and return that same object. Object.seal prevents additions, removals, descriptor changes, and prototype reassignment while retaining writability of existing data properties; Object.freeze adds non-writability, so existing values cannot be reassigned. Neither operation recursively affects referenced objects.

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: The object whose properties and extensibility are restricted.

Object & JSON::Object.freeze and Object..returns: The same object passed to the method.

example.title: Seal versus freeze
example.explanation: Sealing permits changes to writable existing properties, whereas freezing prevents reassignment as well.

useCases.title: Controlled mutable configuration
useCases.scenario: Expose a configuration object whose keys must not be added, removed, or reconfigured, while allowing selected writable values to change.

useCases.title: Shallow immutable state
useCases.scenario: Protect an object from property additions, removals, descriptor changes, and value reassignment at its immediate level.

useCases.title: Object integrity hardening
useCases.scenario: Prevent prototype reassignment and extension of objects crossing a trust boundary.

interview.question: What does Object.seal do?
interview.answer: Object.seal prevents extensions and makes existing properties non-configurable. Existing data properties may still change when their writable attribute is true.
interview.followUp: How does sealing affect the prototype? The prototype chain is unchanged, but the object's [[Prototype]] cannot be reassigned because the object is non-extensible.

interview.question: How does Object.freeze differ from Object.seal?
interview.answer: Object.freeze also prevents extensions and makes existing properties non-configurable, but it additionally makes data properties non-writable. Therefore existing data values cannot be reassigned.
interview.followUp: Is freeze deep? No. Its effect applies only to the object's immediate properties, not objects reachable through those properties.

interview.question: What do these methods return, and how do violations behave?
interview.answer: Both methods return the object passed to them rather than creating a copy. Attempts to violate the restrictions can fail silently or throw TypeError, especially in strict mode.
interview.followUp: What happens with primitive arguments? In ES2015 and later, non-object arguments are returned unchanged because primitives are already immutable.

keyPoints: Object.seal fixes the property set and prevents existing properties from being removed or reconfigured.
Sealing does not automatically prevent assignment to writable data properties.
Sealing does not alter inherited properties or the prototype chain itself.
gotchas: Adding or deleting properties on a sealed object fails; depending on strictness, the failure is silent or a TypeError.

Object & JSON::Object.fromEntries.summary: Builds a new object from an iterable of key-value pairs, such as a Map or an array of pairs. Keys can be strings or symbols.
Object & JSON::Object.fromEntries.explanation: Object.fromEntries() consumes an iterable whose items each provide a property key and value. It creates a new ordinary object and assigns each pair as a property; the key may be a string or symbol, and later entries can replace earlier values for the same key.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: An iterable whose yielded items are two-element array-like objects. Position 0 supplies a string or symbol property key, and position 1 supplies its value.

Object & JSON::Object.fromEntries.returns: A new object whose properties are supplied by the iterable's entries.

example.title: Convert a Map to an object
example.explanation: Converts a Map's key-value pairs into a plain object.

useCases.title: Map conversion
useCases.scenario: Convert a Map into a plain object for APIs or object-based utilities.

useCases.title: Entry-pipeline transformations
useCases.scenario: Transform or filter entries with array methods, then materialize the result as an object.

useCases.title: Symbol-keyed properties
useCases.scenario: Construct an object while retaining symbol property keys.

interview.question: What input does Object.fromEntries() accept?
interview.answer: It accepts an iterable that yields two-element array-like items. The first element becomes the property key and the second becomes its value; the result is a new object.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from Object.entries()? Object.entries() extracts own enumerable string-keyed properties, while fromEntries() can create symbol-keyed properties.

interview.question: How can a Map be converted into an object?
interview.answer: A Map works directly because it is iterable and yields [key, value] pairs. An array of such pairs works as well, so the method is useful for converting either representation into an object.
interview.followUp: What happens with duplicate keys? The later property definition determines the final value for that key.

interview.question: Does Object.fromEntries() construct instances of a supplied this value?
interview.answer: The method creates a new ordinary object whose properties come from the iterable's entries. It does not use this, so borrowing or calling it with another constructor does not change the result's object type.
interview.followUp: Can the resulting object contain symbol properties? Yes, because the property-key position may contain a symbol.

keyPoints: Use it to turn an iterable of pairs into a newly created object.
Valid sources include arrays of pairs and Map instances, as long as they are iterable.
Each key may be either a string or a symbol.
The second item in each entry becomes that property's value.
The return value is a new object populated from the supplied entries.
The iterable must yield items with two accessible positions: key first, value second.
gotchas: Every item must provide key and value positions, conventionally as a two-element array; an item without the required structure is invalid.
Calling the method with a different constructor does not make an instance of that constructor; it still creates an ordinary object.
Unlike Object.entries(), the method preserves symbol keys when constructing the result.

Object & JSON::Object.keys, values and e.summary: Read an object's own enumerable string-keyed properties as an array of keys, values, or [key, value] pairs. Use Object.keys(), Object.values(), or Object.entries() according to the representation needed.
Object & JSON::Object.keys, values and e.explanation: These static methods convert an object's own enumerable string-keyed properties into arrays. Object.keys returns property names, Object.values returns corresponding values, and Object.entries returns two-item key-value arrays; inherited and non-enumerable properties are excluded.

parameters.name: obj / O
parameters.description: The value to convert to an object and inspect for own enumerable string-keyed properties.

Object & JSON::Object.keys, values and e.returns: Object.keys returns an array of strings; Object.values returns an array of property values; Object.entries returns an array of [key, value] arrays.

example.title: Read an object's enumerable properties
example.explanation: Use the method that matches the data needed: property names, property values, or pairs of both.

useCases.title: Collect keys
useCases.scenario: Need a list of property names for validation, display, or lookup.

useCases.title: Collect values
useCases.scenario: Need to transform or aggregate an object's property values.

useCases.title: Process entries
useCases.scenario: Need to filter or map properties while retaining both names and values.

interview.question: What does Object.keys return?
interview.answer: Object.keys returns an array of an object's own enumerable string-keyed property names. It excludes inherited and non-enumerable properties.
interview.followUp: How would you obtain the values instead? Use Object.values, which returns the corresponding own enumerable string-keyed property values.

interview.question: How do Object.values and Object.entries differ?
interview.answer: Object.values returns values, while Object.entries returns arrays containing each key and its value. Both operate on own enumerable string-keyed properties.
interview.followUp: Why might Object.entries be preferable for a loop? It provides the key and value together, avoiding a separate lookup.

interview.question: What ordering and ownership rules apply?
interview.answer: The returned array follows the same property order used by a for...in loop for the object's enumerable own string-keyed properties. The methods themselves do not traverse the prototype chain.
interview.followUp: What happens with null? ToObject cannot convert it, so the call throws a TypeError before producing an array.

keyPoints: Object.keys produces property-name strings for properties owned directly by the object.
Choose Object.values when the keys are not needed and only the property values should be collected.
Choose Object.entries when each result must retain its key alongside its value.
The output order follows the object's enumerable-property iteration order.
The methods accept non-object arguments by converting them to object wrappers when conversion is possible.
Enumerability controls whether these object-reading methods include a property.
gotchas: Passing null or undefined throws a TypeError because they cannot be converted to objects.
Primitive inputs are coerced to objects; strings can produce indexed keys, while other primitives produce empty arrays.
The methods do not include inherited properties, unlike for...in.

Object & JSON::structuredClone.sourceTitle: Window: structuredClone () method - Web APIs | MDN
Object & JSON::structuredClone.summary: Creates a deep clone of a structured-cloneable value, including supported built-ins such as Map, Set, Date, and typed arrays. Transferable resources can optionally be moved to the result instead of copied.
Object & JSON::structuredClone.explanation: structuredClone() creates a deep copy using the structured clone algorithm. It supports circular references and many built-in data types, while optionally transferring transferable resources instead of duplicating them.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The object to be cloned; it can be any structured-cloneable type.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional options object containing transfer, an array of transferable objects moved to the result rather than cloned.

Object & JSON::structuredClone.returns: A deep copy of the original value.

example.title: Clone nested built-in values
example.explanation: The clone has independent nested values, so changing its Set or typed array does not change the source.

useCases.title: Copy application data
useCases.scenario: Create independent state snapshots containing nested objects and built-in collections.

useCases.title: Clone cyclic structures
useCases.scenario: Duplicate cyclic graphs that JSON.stringify() cannot represent.

useCases.title: Transfer binary data
useCases.scenario: Move an ArrayBuffer to another result without paying for a duplicate buffer.

useCases.title: Exchange structured data
useCases.scenario: Prepare values for worker messaging or other APIs that use structured cloning.

interview.question: What does structuredClone() do, and how does it differ from JSON serialization?
interview.answer: It takes a value and returns a deep copy produced by the structured clone algorithm. Unlike a JSON round trip, it can handle circular references and supported built-in values such as Map, Set, Date, and typed arrays.
interview.followUp: What happens to an ArrayBuffer when it is listed in transfer? It is moved to the clone and detached from the original rather than copied.

interview.question: What are the arguments to structuredClone()?
interview.answer: The first argument is the value to clone. The optional second argument contains transfer, an array of transferable objects that should be moved to the result instead of cloned.
interview.followUp: Can a Uint8Array itself be transferred? No; transfer its underlying ArrayBuffer instead.

interview.question: When can structuredClone() fail or lose information?
interview.answer: It throws DataCloneError when any part of the input is not serializable, including unsupported values such as functions or DOM nodes. Symbols are also not among the supported primitive types.
interview.followUp: Are class instances fully preserved? No; the prototype chain is not duplicated, and class private elements are not cloned.

keyPoints: The operation recursively copies supported complex values instead of merely copying the outer object.
Circular references are supported because previously visited objects are tracked during traversal.
Map, Date, Set, typed arrays, and plain objects are among the supported values.
Most primitive values can be cloned, but symbols are excluded.
The return value is an independent deep copy of the supplied value.
The transfer option can move transferable resources instead of duplicating them.
gotchas: Functions cannot be cloned; attempting to clone one raises a DataCloneError.
Cloning does not preserve property descriptors, accessors, or similar metadata.
Custom prototype chains are not reproduced in the clone.
A regular expression's lastIndex value is lost during cloning.

Promise API::Promise.race and Promise.an.summary: `Promise.race()` settles from the first input to settle, whether fulfilled or rejected. `Promise.any()` returns the first fulfillment and rejects with an `AggregateError` only when every input rejects.
Promise API::Promise.race and Promise.an.explanation: Both methods accept an iterable whose values are resolved as promises or thenables. `race()` settles asynchronously according to the first item to settle, whether fulfillment or rejection; `any()` fulfills with the first fulfillment and rejects only after every item rejects, reporting their reasons in an `AggregateError`.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: An iterable, such as an Array, whose values are treated as promises; thenables are resolved and non-thenables are used as values.

Promise API::Promise.race and Promise.an.returns: Each method returns a Promise. `Promise.race()` settles asynchronously with the first input settlement; `Promise.any()` fulfills with the first fulfillment or rejects with an `AggregateError` when all inputs reject.

example.title: Race completion or choose the first success
example.explanation: `Promise.race()` chooses the first operation to settle, while `Promise.any()` ignores rejections until one operation fulfills.

useCases.title: First completion wins
useCases.scenario: Use `Promise.race()` when whichever operation finishes first should decide the result, including failures.

useCases.title: First successful alternative
useCases.scenario: Use `Promise.any()` when several alternatives can satisfy the request and failures should be ignored until all alternatives fail.

useCases.title: Redundant async sources
useCases.scenario: Provide multiple service endpoints or fallback sources and choose the first usable response.

interview.question: What does `Promise.race()` do?
interview.answer: `Promise.race()` returns a promise that adopts the eventual state of the first input to settle. Therefore, the first fulfillment resolves it and the first rejection rejects it.
interview.followUp: How does an empty iterable behave? It leaves the returned promise pending forever.

interview.question: How does `Promise.any()` differ from `Promise.race()`?
interview.answer: `Promise.any()` fulfills with the first input promise that fulfills and ignores earlier rejections. It rejects only if every input rejects, using an `AggregateError` containing the rejection reasons.
interview.followUp: What happens with an empty iterable? It rejects with an `AggregateError`, because no input can fulfill.

interview.question: What inputs do these methods accept?
interview.answer: Both methods accept an iterable, such as an array, and await its values, so thenables are also resolved and non-promises are treated as values. The returned promise settles asynchronously for `race()`; `any()` reports collective failure through `AggregateError`.
interview.followUp: What does `Promise.race()` do with non-promise values? It can settle based on the first such value encountered in the iterable.

keyPoints: `Promise.any(iterable)` returns the value from the first input that fulfills.
After `Promise.any()` finds a fulfillment, its result is decided without waiting for remaining inputs.
The iterable may contain promises, thenables, or ordinary values; each value is normalized for the operation.
For `Promise.race()`, an ordinary value or already settled promise can determine the outcome before later inputs.
gotchas: An empty iterable makes `Promise.race()` remain pending indefinitely.
`Promise.any()` rejects for an empty iterable and when no input fulfills.
Handle `Promise.any()` failure as `AggregateError`; its `errors` property contains the individual rejection reasons.
Even already settled inputs do not make `Promise.race()` settle synchronously.

Promise API::Promise.resolve, reject and.summary: Promise.resolve normalizes values and thenables into promises, while Promise.reject creates a new rejected promise. then returns a new promise, so handler results, adopted promises, and errors can form a chain.
Promise API::Promise.resolve, reject and.explanation: Promise.resolve converts a value or promise-like object into a promise, while Promise.reject creates a newly rejected promise. Calling then schedules fulfillment and rejection callbacks and returns a distinct promise whose state follows the callback result or thrown error.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Value or thenable to normalize into a promise.

parameters.name: reason
parameters.description: Reason for the rejection.

parameters.name: onFulfilled
parameters.description: Callback for fulfillment; optional.

parameters.name: onRejected
parameters.description: Callback for rejection; optional.

Promise API::Promise.resolve, reject and.returns: Promise.resolve returns a promise resolved with or adopting the supplied value. Promise.reject returns a newly rejected promise. Promise.prototype.then returns another promise whose outcome depends on its handlers.

example.title: Settled promises and chaining
example.code:
const fulfilled = Promise.resolve(21);
const result = fulfilled
  .then((value) => value * 2)
  .then((value) => `result: ${value}`);

Promise.reject(new Error("failed"))
  .then(
    () => "not called",
    (error) => error.message,
  )
  .then(console.log); // failed

result.then(console.log); // result: 42
example.explanation: The first chain transforms a fulfillment value through successive handlers. The second starts rejected, handles the reason in its rejection callback, and fulfills with that callback's returned string.

useCases.title: Normalize mixed inputs
useCases.scenario: Convert a synchronous value or promise-like result to one consistent promise interface.

useCases.title: Represent failure
useCases.scenario: Create an immediately rejected result for validation or failure paths.

useCases.title: Build promise chains
useCases.scenario: Transform asynchronous results step by step while propagating success and failure.

interview.question: What does Promise.resolve do with different kinds of input?
interview.answer: Promise.resolve(value) returns a promise. A promise argument is returned, a thenable is adopted, and another value produces a fulfilled promise.
interview.followUp: What happens with Promise.resolve(Promise.reject(error))? It returns the rejected promise because resolution adopts the input promise's state.

interview.question: How does Promise.reject differ from Promise.resolve?
interview.answer: Promise.reject(reason) always returns a new rejected promise containing the supplied reason. Unlike Promise.resolve, it does not reuse an existing Promise instance.
interview.followUp: What if reason is already a rejected promise? The new promise is rejected with that promise as its rejection reason; it is not the same promise.

interview.question: How does then enable chaining?
interview.answer: then takes optional fulfillment and rejection callbacks and immediately returns a new promise. The returned promise follows the callback's returned value, adopted thenable, thrown error, or rejected promise.
interview.followUp: What happens when a callback is not a function? It is ignored, so the prior fulfillment or rejection passes through to the next promise.

keyPoints: Promise.resolve(value) normalizes a value into a promise; a non-thenable value makes the result fulfilled with that value.
Thenables are assimilated: Promise.resolve invokes their then method and adopts the state they eventually produce.
Promise.reject(reason) creates a rejected promise whose rejection reason is the supplied argument.
gotchas: “Resolved” does not necessarily mean fulfilled: resolving with a rejected or pending promise adopts that promise's state.
Promise.reject does not reuse an existing promise passed as its reason; it always creates a new wrapper.

Shipping JavaScript::Feature detection.summary: Check whether a runtime supports a capability before using it, then choose the supported implementation or a fallback. This avoids failures when newer APIs or language features are unavailable.
Shipping JavaScript::Feature detection.explanation: Feature detection tests whether a runtime exposes a capability before dependent code runs. Use a supported capability check, then select the primary implementation or a fallback so unsupported environments remain functional.

example.title: Checking an API member
example.explanation: Checks whether the runtime exposes the geolocation entry point before calling it; otherwise, it uses an alternative path.

useCases.title: Guard optional browser APIs
useCases.scenario: A web application wants to use an API that may not exist in every browser.

useCases.title: Select element behavior
useCases.scenario: A component needs to work across runtimes with different element capabilities.

useCases.title: Choose a fallback
useCases.scenario: A site needs to preserve functionality when a preferred capability is unavailable.

interview.question: What is feature detection?
interview.answer: Feature detection determines whether a runtime supports a capability, then conditionally runs suitable code. This lets supported and unsupported browsers receive working behavior instead of an error.
interview.followUp: How would you detect an API exposed as an object member? Test the member on its parent object, such as using `"geolocation" in navigator`.

interview.question: How can JavaScript detect an object-based API?
interview.answer: A common pattern is checking whether a method or property exists on its parent object before using it. For example, checking `"geolocation" in navigator` guards access to the Geolocation API.
interview.followUp: What if existence alone is insufficient? Invoke or inspect the feature and verify the specific return value or retained assigned value.

interview.question: How can browser features be detected when they are element-based?
interview.answer: Create an element in memory and inspect its relevant property or method. Depending on the feature, detection may also assign a value and check whether the element retained it.
interview.followUp: Why prefer this over browser identification? Capability checks select behavior from actual support, whereas browser identity does not directly establish that the capability works.

keyPoints: Run a capability test before choosing the implementation that depends on it.
Use the test result to choose code that preserves a usable experience.
Detection commonly relies on checking object members, element properties, method results, or retained assignments.
For element features, create a temporary element and inspect whether the needed property exists.
gotchas: Detect capabilities rather than assuming that a particular runtime supports the code.
Some features require more than an existence check: call a detectable method and validate its result.

Shipping JavaScript::Modules in browsers.summary: JavaScript modules expose selected values with export and consume them with import. Browser and Node.js hosts resolve module specifiers differently, so portable ESM requires explicit, runtime-compatible paths and browser import maps where needed.
Shipping JavaScript::Modules in browsers.explanation: An ECMAScript module is a file whose exports form its public interface and whose imports consume other modules' read-only live bindings. The language defines the declarations, while the host resolves each module specifier: browsers use URL-based resolution, and Node.js also supports package and built-in-module conventions. In browser HTML, type="module" marks the entry script.
Shipping JavaScript::Modules in browsers.syntax: export { name }; import { name } from "./module.js"; <script type="module" src="./main.js"></script>

example.title: A browser ESM boundary
example.explanation: Save the files together and open index.html from a web server. The HTML module script enables import/export, and the relative specifier includes the file extension.

useCases.title: Browser application boundaries
useCases.scenario: Split browser code into files with explicit relative URLs and a module entry script.

useCases.title: Package API boundaries
useCases.scenario: Publish a package whose public API is defined by its exports and consumed through supported package specifiers.

useCases.title: Browser dependency mapping
useCases.scenario: Use import maps to provide stable browser-facing names while retaining URL targets.

interview.question: What does a static import provide?
interview.answer: Static import declarations are only valid in modules and must appear at top level. They create read-only live bindings to exports, rather than copying values into the importing module.
interview.followUp: How can code load a module conditionally? Use dynamic import(), which returns a promise and can be evaluated from a potentially non-module environment.

interview.question: How do you start an ESM graph in a browser?
interview.answer: In HTML, add type="module" to the script element. The browser then treats the referenced file as a module, enabling import and export declarations.
interview.followUp: What happens to a relative browser specifier? It is resolved as a URL relative to the current module URL, so the path and filename must be valid.

interview.question: Why are import paths runtime-dependent?
interview.answer: Module specifier resolution is host-defined. Browsers use URL-oriented rules, while Node.js additionally supports node: URLs for built-ins and bare package specifiers resolved through node_modules.
interview.followUp: Why can a path that works in Node fail in a browser? A bare package name or extensionless path may not be a browser-resolvable URL without suitable mapping or a complete relative URL.

keyPoints: Exports define the values that another module may consume; an unexported declaration remains private to its module.
An importing module selects the named, default, namespace, or side-effect form appropriate to the dependency.
In browsers, an import map can map a convenient specifier to the URL used to resolve the dependency.
Import-map targets must resolve to absolute or relative URLs, keeping browser module loading URL-based.
Node-style bare package names use package resolution rather than browser-relative URL resolution.
gotchas: Browser-style relative imports need the explicit filename and extension; do not rely on directory or extension inference.
A classic script cannot contain static ESM declarations; load the entry point as a module.
Do not assume one universal resolution algorithm: browser and Node environments can interpret the same specifier differently.

Shipping JavaScript::TC39 proposal stage.summary: TC39 proposal stages express how mature a JavaScript feature is, from early exploration through standard-ready completion. A stage is not a guarantee that a feature has shipped in every engine; check runtime support separately.
Shipping JavaScript::TC39 proposal stage.explanation: TC39 proposals move through six stages: an initial strawperson stage followed by maturity stages 1 through 5? The fetched process page describes stages 0 through 4, with Stage 4 meaning a feature is complete and ready for inclusion in the standard. A stage label indicates proposal maturity; it does not by itself guarantee that every runtime supports the feature.

example.title: Using a standardized feature
example.explanation: This runnable code uses an established ECMAScript feature; proposal stage labels describe standardization maturity, not a separate runtime syntax.

useCases.title: Evaluating proposal maturity
useCases.scenario: Assessing whether a proposed JavaScript feature is mature enough to evaluate in a project.

useCases.title: Communicating compatibility risk
useCases.scenario: Explaining why an experimental feature may change or disappear.

useCases.title: Checking shipping status
useCases.scenario: Separating committee status from actual browser or runtime availability.

interview.question: How many stages does the TC39 process have, and what does Stage 4 mean?
interview.answer: TC39 uses six stages: a strawperson stage and five maturity stages. The process page labels the maturity levels 0 through 4, where Stage 0 is new work and Stage 4 is complete and ready for standard inclusion.
interview.followUp: What evidence is required at Stage 1? A champion or champion group, a problem statement and proposed shape, semantic discussion, cross-cutting concerns, implementation challenges, and a public proposal repository.

interview.question: What does Stage 2 communicate about a proposal?
interview.answer: Stage 2 means the committee has selected a preferred solution or solution space, but the design can still change substantially. It includes high-level APIs and syntax, usage examples, and initial specification text covering major semantics.
interview.followUp: What distinguishes Stage 2.7? The proposal is approved in principle and complete enough that further progress depends on validation from tests, implementations, or usage.

interview.question: Does Stage 3 mean a feature has shipped?
interview.answer: Stage 3 means the proposal has been recommended for implementation. It is therefore a strong signal of maturity, but it does not mean the feature is already part of the ECMAScript standard.
interview.followUp: What is the final maturity stage? Stage 4 means the feature is complete and ready to be included in the standard.

keyPoints: TC39 describes six stages overall: one strawperson stage plus five maturity stages.
Stage 0 identifies a new proposal that is not yet being considered by the committee.
Stage 1 means the committee is actively examining the problem, possible solutions, and broader concerns.
Stage 2 records a preferred design, while allowing significant changes before standardization.
Stage 2.7 indicates an essentially complete solution that now needs validation through tests, implementations, or usage.
Stage 3 signals that implementation is recommended, not that the feature is universally available.
Stage 4 is the completion point for the proposal process and prepares a feature for standard inclusion.
gotchas: Stage 2 is not a promise of eventual standardization: even a preferred design can still be abandoned.
Stage 3 is not the same as shipped everywhere; it means the proposal is close to completion and recommended for implementation.

String methods::String.prototype.localeC.summary: Compares two strings according to locale-sensitive sort rules. It returns a negative, positive, or zero number based on whether the receiver comes before, after, or is equivalent to the supplied string.
String methods::String.prototype.localeC.explanation: Call this method on a reference string and pass the string to compare with it. Optional locale and options arguments select language-sensitive comparison behavior; the result is negative, positive, or zero according to the strings’ relative sort order.
String methods::String.prototype.localeC.syntax:
localeCompare(compareString)
localeCompare(compareString, locales)
localeCompare(compareString, locales, options)

parameters.name: compareString
parameters.description: The string to compare with the reference string.

parameters.name: locales
parameters.description: Optional BCP 47 language tag or array of tags selecting locale conventions.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional object controlling comparison behavior, such as sensitivity and numeric ordering.

String methods::String.prototype.localeC.returns: A negative number when the reference string precedes compareString, a positive number when it follows it, or 0 when they are equivalent.

example.title: Locale-aware sorting
example.explanation: Sorts names using English locale rules while treating case and accents as less significant.

useCases.title: Locale-aware sorting
useCases.scenario: Ordering names, labels, or translated text in a user-facing list.

useCases.title: Localized equality checks
useCases.scenario: Comparing text while configuring case or accent sensitivity.

useCases.title: Reusable collation
useCases.scenario: Sorting many strings with one consistent locale and option set.

interview.question: What does localeCompare return?
interview.answer: It compares the reference string with compareString using locale-sensitive ordering. A negative result means the reference comes first, a positive result means it comes later, and zero means the strings are equivalent for the comparison.
interview.followUp: How would you optimize sorting a large array? Create one Intl.Collator with the desired locales and options, then pass its compare method to sort.

interview.question: What are the method’s arguments used for?
interview.answer: The method accepts compareString, followed optionally by locales and options. These optional arguments control the language and collation conventions used for the comparison.
interview.followUp: How can you make equality less sensitive to case or accents? Use an Intl.Collator or localeCompare with options such as sensitivity: "accent" or sensitivity: "base".

interview.question: How should its result be used in sorting code?
interview.answer: It is useful in sort callbacks because its sign supplies the ordering relation required by sorting. The numeric magnitude is implementation-dependent, so a callback should return the method result directly or inspect only its sign.
interview.followUp: Why should code avoid checking result === -1? Implementations may return any negative number rather than exactly -1.

keyPoints: It compares the receiver with another string and communicates their relative locale-aware order through a number.
The full call can specify the comparison string, requested locales, and collation options.
A negative result means the receiver sorts before the argument.
A positive result means the receiver sorts after the argument.
Zero indicates that the two values are equivalent under the comparison settings.
Where supported, the method uses the internationalization collation machinery provided by Intl.Collator.
gotchas: Only the sign of the returned number is portable; code should test whether the result is below, above, or equal to zero.
For repeated comparisons, construct an Intl.Collator once and use its compare method instead of repeatedly invoking localeCompare.
Results depend on the selected locale and options, so omit them only when the runtime’s default behavior is appropriate.

String methods::String.prototype.matchAl.summary: Returns an iterator over every match of a pattern, including capture groups and each match's position. Consume it with `for...of`, spread syntax, or `Array.from()`.

It returns a one-use iterator whose yielded arrays follow `RegExp.prototype.exec()` results, including captures, the match index, and—when applicable—named groups. A regular-expression argument must include `g`; other values are converted to a global regular expression unless they provide their own `Symbol.matchAll` method.

parameters.description: A regular expression, or an object with a `Symbol.matchAll` method. A non-RegExp without that method is converted to `new RegExp(regexp, "g")`; a RegExp must use `g`.

String methods::String.prototype.matchAl.returns: An iterable, non-restartable iterator of match arrays; it is empty when there are no matches. A `TypeError` is thrown when a RegExp argument lacks the `g` flag.

example.title: Read matches, captures, and positions
example.explanation: Iterates over every global match and reads the full match, its captured identifier, and the starting position.

useCases.scenario: A global pattern captures repeated records while each result supplies the full match, captures, and index.

useCases.title: Extract captured fields
useCases.scenario: Named or numbered captures can be read from every occurrence without manually advancing a regular expression.

useCases.title: Process matches incrementally
useCases.scenario: Iterator consumption fits streaming-style loops and avoids constructing an array until needed.

useCases.scenario: Spread or `Array.from()` materializes the iterator for sorting, counting, or repeated access.

interview.question: What does `String.prototype.matchAll()` return?
interview.answer: `matchAll()` returns an iterator rather than a single match array. Each yielded value has the same structure as `RegExp.prototype.exec()`, so it contains the complete match, capture groups, and the match position.
interview.followUp: How would you process the iterator more than once? Materialize it first, for example with `const matches = [...text.matchAll(re)]`, then iterate over `matches` as needed.

interview.question: Why must the regular expression contain `g`?
interview.answer: A RegExp supplied to `matchAll()` must have the global `g` flag. Otherwise the method throws `TypeError`, because the operation is defined to enumerate all matches.
interview.followUp: What happens with a non-RegExp argument? Unless it supplies `Symbol.matchAll`, it is converted using `new RegExp(value, 'g')`.

interview.question: How can `matchAll()` support custom matching behavior?
interview.answer: The method delegates matching to the argument's `Symbol.matchAll` method when one is available. This permits custom matcher objects and means their method's return value becomes the result of `matchAll()`.
interview.followUp: What is the standard RegExp implementation? `RegExp.prototype[Symbol.matchAll]()` performs the actual matching and produces the iterator.

keyPoints: It enumerates every match and preserves the pattern's capture groups.
Each result is an exec-style array, so `result[0]` is the complete match and later indexes hold captures.
The string method primarily dispatches to the argument's `Symbol.matchAll` hook.
It replaces the traditional repeated `exec()` loop with direct iterator consumption.
Use `for...of`, spread syntax, or `Array.from()` to consume the matches.
Objects implementing `Symbol.matchAll` can define matching behavior without being RegExp instances.
For custom matchers, the hook's returned value is exposed directly by the string method.
gotchas: A RegExp argument without the `g` flag throws `TypeError`; add `g` even when only one match is expected.
The returned iterator is consumable only once. Save the results with `[...text.matchAll(pattern)]` if you need to traverse them repeatedly.
A string or other non-RegExp argument is converted with a global flag, which can differ from passing an explicitly configured regular expression.

String methods::String.prototype.normali.summary: String.prototype.normalize() converts a string to a chosen Unicode Normalization Form. Normalize equivalent strings to the same form before comparing them.
String methods::String.prototype.normali.explanation: normalize() converts the calling string to a selected Unicode Normalization Form. With no argument or with undefined, it uses NFC; otherwise it converts the argument to a string, accepts only NFC, NFD, NFKC, or NFKD, and throws RangeError for any other form.

parameters.name: form
parameters.description: Specifies the Unicode Normalization Form. It may be "NFC", "NFD", "NFKC", or "NFKD"; omitted or undefined selects NFC.

String methods::String.prototype.normali.returns: A string containing the Unicode Normalization Form of the given string.

example.title: Compare canonically equivalent strings
example.explanation: Normalize both strings to the same Unicode form before comparing them.

useCases.scenario: Compare user-entered text that may encode the same character with different Unicode code-point sequences.

useCases.title: Canonical text representation
useCases.scenario: Create a consistent representation before storing or indexing text.

useCases.title: Compatibility-aware matching
useCases.scenario: Handle compatibility-equivalent characters when application rules treat them alike.

interview.question: What does String.prototype.normalize do?
interview.answer: It returns the Unicode Normalization Form of the string. If form is omitted or undefined, the method uses NFC; the accepted explicit forms are NFC, NFD, NFKC, and NFKD.
interview.followUp: What happens for normalize("nfc")? It throws RangeError because the form must exactly match one of the four permitted uppercase names.

interview.question: How do NFC, NFD, NFKC, and NFKD differ?
interview.answer: NFC performs canonical decomposition followed by canonical composition, while NFD performs canonical decomposition only. Both provide forms for canonically equivalent strings.
interview.followUp: How do NFKC and NFKD differ? They use compatibility decomposition; NFKC composes afterward, whereas NFKD remains decomposed.

interview.question: Why normalize strings before comparing them?
interview.answer: Two canonically equivalent sequences can use different code-point sequences for the same character, so direct equality may fail. Normalizing both strings to the same canonical form makes comparison reliable for that equivalence.
interview.followUp: Does JavaScript normalize strings automatically for ordinary equality? No; explicit normalize() is needed, although localeCompare internally normalizes string values.

keyPoints: The method produces a normalized string value rather than modifying the original string.
Calling normalize() without an argument is equivalent to requesting NFC.
NFC creates the composed canonical form after decomposing canonically equivalent sequences.
NFD leaves the result in canonical decomposed form.
NFKC applies compatibility decomposition and then produces a composed result.
NFKD applies compatibility decomposition without canonical composition afterward.
Use NFC or NFD when the comparison should preserve canonical equivalence rather than broader compatibility equivalence.
gotchas: The form argument is case-sensitive and cannot contain surrounding whitespace; unsupported values raise RangeError.
NFKC and NFKD can make compatibility-equivalent strings alike even when they are not canonically equivalent, so choose them only when that equivalence is appropriate.

String methods::String.prototype.replace.summary: Use replace() to substitute the first string match, or replaceAll() to substitute every match. Either accepts replacement text or a function, and both return a new string without changing the source.
String methods::String.prototype.replace.explanation: Call replace(pattern, replacement) when only the first string match should change, or replaceAll(pattern, replacement) when every match should change. The pattern may be a string or a replacement-capable object such as a regular expression, and the replacement may be text or a function whose result supplies the replacement.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: The search pattern: a string or an object with Symbol.replace, commonly a RegExp.

parameters.name: replacement
parameters.description: Replacement text, or a function invoked for each match to compute replacement text.

String methods::String.prototype.replace.returns: A new string with the pattern's matches replaced by the replacement.

example.title: Replace one match or all matches
example.explanation: Both methods return new strings; the original remains unchanged. A string pattern is replaced once by replace() and at every occurrence by replaceAll().

useCases.title: Single substitution
useCases.scenario: Change one known occurrence while preserving later occurrences.

useCases.title: Global literal replacement
useCases.scenario: Normalize or redact every occurrence of a literal token.

useCases.title: Callback-based transformation
useCases.scenario: Compute replacement text from each matched value.

interview.question: How do replace() and replaceAll() differ?
interview.answer: replace() returns a new string and, with a string pattern, replaces only the first occurrence. replaceAll() returns a new string and replaces every occurrence of a string pattern.
interview.followUp: What happens with a regular-expression pattern? replaceAll() requires that the regular expression have the global g flag; otherwise it throws TypeError.

interview.question: What forms can the replacement argument take?
interview.answer: The replacement can be either a string or a function. The function is called for each match, and its return value becomes that match's replacement text.
interview.followUp: How can a replacement function transform matches? Use its match-related arguments and return the desired text for each invocation.

interview.question: What can be used as the pattern?
interview.answer: The pattern can be a string or an object providing Symbol.replace, with RegExp being the usual example. Values without that method are converted to strings.
interview.followUp: What does a custom Symbol.replace method control? Its result becomes the result returned by replaceAll() when the pattern supplies that method.

keyPoints: replaceAll() produces a new string after replacing every match of its pattern.
Both methods support string or regular-expression-style patterns, and replacement text or a callback.
The source string is immutable from the perspective of these operations; the result contains the edits.
A pattern without Symbol.replace is converted to a string before matching.
Replacement-capable pattern objects can define the matching and replacement behavior through Symbol.replace.
gotchas: With replaceAll(), a regular-expression pattern must use the global g flag; otherwise JavaScript throws TypeError.
Neither method changes the original string. Store the returned value if the replacement is needed later.
replace() with a string pattern changes only the first occurrence, whereas replaceAll() changes every occurrence.

String methods::String.prototype.slice a.summary: Extract a portion of a string with slice() or substring(), using a start index and an optional exclusive end index. They differ mainly in negative-index behavior and in handling reversed bounds.
String methods::String.prototype.slice a.explanation: Both methods return a new string containing characters from a start index up to, but excluding, an optional end index. slice() supports indexes counted from the end with negative values, whereas substring() converts negative or NaN arguments to zero and swaps the arguments when the start exceeds the end.
String methods::String.prototype.slice a.syntax:
slice(indexStart)
slice(indexStart, indexEnd)
substring(indexStart)
substring(indexStart, indexEnd)

parameters.name: indexStart
parameters.description: The zero-based position of the first character to include. slice() interprets negative values from the end; substring() treats negative or NaN values as zero.

parameters.name: indexEnd
parameters.description: Optional zero-based position of the first character to exclude. If omitted, extraction continues to the end; handling otherwise depends on the method.

String methods::String.prototype.slice a.returns: A new string containing the extracted section.

example.title: Extracting text with slice and substring
example.code:
const text = "JavaScript";

console.log(text.slice(4, 10));      // "Script"
console.log(text.slice(-6));         // "Script"
console.log(text.substring(4, 10));  // "Script"
console.log(text.substring(10, 4));  // "Script" (arguments swapped)
console.log(text.slice(10, 4));       // "" (start is after end)
example.explanation: Both methods use an inclusive start position and an exclusive end position, but they handle unusual indexes differently.

useCases.title: Extract a bounded range
useCases.scenario: Select a fixed range using zero-based boundaries, such as a file extension or a displayed prefix.

useCases.title: Read from the end
useCases.scenario: Use a negative slice index to obtain a suffix without first calculating the string length.

useCases.title: Normalize reversed bounds
useCases.scenario: Use substring() when reversed bounds should be normalized automatically.

interview.question: How do slice() and substring() differ in their index handling?
interview.answer: Both methods return characters beginning at the start index and stop before the end index. slice() interprets negative indexes relative to the string's end, while substring() treats negative or NaN arguments as zero.
interview.followUp: What happens when the first index is greater than the second? substring() swaps them; slice() returns an empty string.

interview.question: How are negative indexes handled?
interview.answer: With slice(), a negative index is offset from the string's end and clamped at zero. For substring(), a negative argument is treated as zero.
interview.followUp: What does substring(-3, 2) do? It behaves like substring(0, 2), because -3 is converted to zero.

interview.question: What is the effect of omitting the end index?
interview.answer: The end index is optional for both methods. If it is omitted or undefined, extraction continues through the end of the string.
interview.followUp: What does an end index equal to the string length do? It also extracts through the end, because the boundary is exclusive and at the length limit.

keyPoints: slice() creates and returns a new string containing the selected section; it does not change the source string.
The first argument identifies the first character included in the result.
The optional second argument marks the exclusive upper boundary.
slice() can select from the end by using a negative start index.
slice() continues to the string's end when no usable end boundary is supplied.

String methods::String.prototype.split.summary: String.prototype.split() searches a string for a separator or pattern and returns the intervening pieces as an array. An optional limit restricts how many entries are included.
String methods::String.prototype.split.explanation: The method searches the calling string from left to right for a separator and returns the intervening substrings in an array. The separator may be a string, a regular expression, or another object that supplies a Symbol.split method; an optional limit restricts how many array entries are produced.

parameters.name: separator
parameters.description: The pattern that identifies split positions. It may be undefined, a string, or an object with a Symbol.split method, such as a regular expression.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: An optional non-negative integer limiting the number of substrings included in the returned array.

String methods::String.prototype.split.returns: An array of strings containing the substrings produced by splitting the calling string; regular-expression captures may also appear.

example.title: Split with a string or regular expression
example.explanation: A string separator removes each matching delimiter; a regular expression can also contribute its captured groups to the resulting array.

useCases.title: Tokenize delimited text
useCases.scenario: Parse a delimiter-separated record into fields.

useCases.title: Pattern-based parsing
useCases.scenario: Use a regular expression to divide text while retaining selected delimiters through capture groups.

useCases.title: Bounded splitting
useCases.scenario: Limit processing to the first few resulting segments.

interview.question: What does String.prototype.split do?
interview.answer: split() accepts a separator and an optional limit. It returns an array of substrings formed by searching for the separator from left to right; the separator itself is not included.
interview.followUp: What happens when the separator is an object with Symbol.split? The method calls that splitter with the original string and limit, allowing custom splitting behavior.

interview.question: How do string and regular-expression separators differ?
interview.answer: With a string separator, every occurrence divides the input. With a regular expression, matches divide the input and captured groups are inserted into the returned array.
interview.followUp: How can a separator implement custom behavior? Define a Symbol.split method on the separator object; split delegates to it instead of applying ordinary string handling.

interview.question: How does the limit argument affect the result?
interview.answer: limit is an optional non-negative integer controlling the maximum number of substrings included. If it is zero, the method returns an empty array; text remaining after the limit is omitted.
interview.followUp: Can the result contain fewer entries than limit? Yes. The array can be shorter when the input ends before enough entries are produced.

keyPoints: The method returns an array by locating separator occurrences and placing the text between them into ordered entries.
The separator supports undefined, strings, regular expressions, and custom splitter objects.
The optional limit caps the number of entries added to the result.
A zero limit immediately produces an empty array.
Once the requested entry count is reached, splitting stops.
String separators are removed at each matching location, leaving the surrounding portions as array elements.
gotchas: Capturing parentheses in a regular-expression separator add the captured text, including unmatched captures as undefined, to the result.
An empty input does not always produce an empty array: with a non-empty separator, the result contains one empty string.
Splitting an empty string with an empty string produces [] rather than [""].
A non-string separator without a custom Symbol.split method is converted to text before matching.

String methods::String.prototype.startsW.summary: Use startsWith(), endsWith(), and includes() to test whether a string begins with, ends with, or contains another string. They return booleans and support an optional search position or endpoint.
String methods::String.prototype.startsW.explanation: These case-sensitive methods test a string without returning the matching text: startsWith() checks from a chosen starting index, endsWith() checks against a chosen exclusive end position, and includes() searches from a chosen starting index. Each returns true or false, and an empty search string matches.
String methods::String.prototype.startsW.syntax:
startsWith(searchString)
startsWith(searchString, position)
endsWith(searchString)
endsWith(searchString, endPosition)
includes(searchString)
includes(searchString, position)

parameters.name: searchString
parameters.description: String whose characters are tested or searched for; it cannot be a regular expression.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Optional start index for startsWith() or includes(); defaults to 0.

parameters.name: endPosition
parameters.description: Optional exclusive end position for endsWith(); defaults to the string length.

String methods::String.prototype.startsW.returns: A boolean: true when the specified condition is satisfied, otherwise false.

example.title: Testing string locations
example.code:
const value = "Saturday night plans";

console.log(value.startsWith("Sat"));      // true
console.log(value.endsWith("plans"));      // true
console.log(value.includes("night"));      // true
console.log(value.includes("NIGHT"));      // false
console.log(value.startsWith("night", 9)); // true
example.explanation: Each method returns a boolean. The optional numeric argument sets the relevant search position: the starting index for startsWith() and includes(), or the exclusive end position for endsWith().

interview.question: How do startsWith(), endsWith(), and includes() differ?
interview.answer: startsWith() tests whether the string begins with the search string, while endsWith() tests whether it finishes with it. includes() tests whether the search string occurs anywhere. All three return booleans and compare case-sensitively.
interview.followUp: What does the optional numeric argument do? startsWith() and includes() begin at that position; endsWith() treats it as the exclusive end position of the portion being tested.

interview.question: What are the method signatures and optional arguments?
interview.answer: The signatures are startsWith(searchString, position), endsWith(searchString, endPosition), and includes(searchString, position). The numeric arguments are optional and default to the beginning or the full string, as appropriate.
interview.followUp: What happens if the search argument is a regular expression? The methods reject it instead of performing a regex search.

interview.question: What edge cases should callers remember?
interview.answer: The methods return true when their condition is met and false otherwise. An empty search string returns true, and comparisons are case-sensitive.
interview.followUp: How could a case-insensitive containment test be implemented? Convert both the source and search strings to the same case before calling includes(), while recognizing that case conversion has Unicode-related considerations.

keyPoints: startsWith() checks whether the string begins with the specified characters.
Its optional position identifies where the expected match must start.
A successful result is true, including when the search string is empty; an unsuccessful result is false.
gotchas: The search argument is not a regular expression; passing one throws a TypeError.
Different letter casing does not match.
An empty search string returns true, including for strings where no visible characters are searched.
For startsWith(), an omitted or undefined argument is converted to the string "undefined" rather than treated as a missing search.
